156	## Cycle bookmarks: create and land
157	
158	The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
159	holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
160	([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
161	
162	**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
163	algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
164	and the bookmark derive from one bare title):
165	
166	- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
167	  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
168	- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
169	  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
170	  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
171	- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
172	  ready to be seen.
173	
174	**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
175	`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
176	stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
177	closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
178	rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):
179	
180	1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
181	   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
182	   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
183	   (`@` sits directly above it).
184	2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
185	   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
186	   as it is.
187	3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
188	   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
189	4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
190	   cycle anymore.
191	5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
192	   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
193	   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
194	   disposal once fully merged.
195	
196	- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
197	  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
198	- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
199	  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.
200	
201	**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
202	bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):
203	
204	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
205	  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
206	  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
207	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
208	- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
209	  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
210	
211	## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged
212	
213	A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
214	carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
215	holder.
216	
217	- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
218	- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged

A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
holder.

- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
  locally and remotely

The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Close-out shapes

The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
is one commit and lands as it is:

- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
  by the landing fast-forward itself.
- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.

Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.

13	1. 2t benches accept a 1-CPU pin pool and livelock through spin
14	   handoffs. `core_for` wraps the pin pool (`src/harness.rs`),
15	   so e.g. `iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-2t --pin 8` pins both the main
16	   thread and the spinning echo worker to core 8. Neither side
17	   yields, so every handoff waits for an involuntary preemption
18	   (milliseconds instead of ~200 ns), and the 5×1,000-step cost
19	   estimate alone takes minutes and the run appears hung.
20	   Observed on 3900x 2026-07-26, and `--pin 8,9` behaves normally.
21	   Cost: an apparent hang the user must ^C, with no hint that
22	   the pinning was the cause. The bug requires pinning: an
23	   unpinned run lets the scheduler separate the threads and
24	   behaves normally. Fix direction:
25	   - Track `core_for` requests in `RunCfg` (max `thread_idx`
26	     asked for): thread placement only goes through `core_for`
27	     when pinning is active, so refusing a pool with fewer
28	     unique CPUs than requested placements covers every path
29	     to this bug, with no per-bench thread-count declaration
30	     needed.
31	   - Independently, put a wall-clock deadline on the open-loop
32	     5×1,000-step estimate phase so *any* pathologically slow
33	     bench aborts with a diagnostic instead of hanging.
34	   - Update 2026-08-02 (0.24.0): the deadline half is fixed structurally: the estimate phase is
35	     gone, and every warmup pass is deadlined by the warm cap (`--warm-cap`, default 1.5 s), so
36	     the hang shrinks to a bounded wait ending in an "uncertified" report. The pool-size guard
37	     half remains open (the run still livelocks through the measurement itself).
38	   - Update 2026-09-02 (0.27.0): `cb-seg-2t` joins the spinning 2t set this covers. `cb-chan-2t`
39	     parks and does not.
40	
41	2. `suggest-freq` perturbs the run it measures. Its descent
42	   wraps each candidate's bench in `sample_while`
43	   (`src/freqctl.rs:699`), which spawns an unpinned thread
44	   that wakes about 20 times a second to read
45	   `scaling_cur_freq`. An ordinary run has no such thread.
46	   Measured on 7600x 2026-09-04 with `zcr-mpsc-2t
47	   --blocks=100 --inner 100 -d 60 --pin-cpus 1,2`, three
48	   interleaved reps per arm, every run graded A:
49	   `--pin-freq=4701` read 74.43 / 74.15 / 74.41 ns while
50	   `suggest-freq` at that same 4701 read 62.51 / 62.82 /
51	   62.89, an 18.5% gap. Both reported `4.67->4.67GHz 99%`
52	   and both verified "Delivered 4.66-4.67 GHz". The gap is
53	   real work rather than a display artifact: `outer` was
54	   7.93M against 9.40M in the same 60.8 s, a ratio of 1.185
55	   matching the latency ratio exactly. We think the waker
56	   holds the package out of deep idle and the fabric clock
57	   with it, which is what a cross-core round trip rides.
58	   Cost: a `suggest-freq` bench report cannot be compared
59	   against any ordinary run's, and nothing on the report
60	   says so. Fix direction:
61	   - Reuse the run's own delivered-clock series instead of
62	     sampling separately. Every run already records one
63	     (`clock_t_ns` / `clock_cpu` / `clock_khz` in the
64	     record, and the settle cell is built from it), and that
65	     path demonstrably does not perturb, since the plain
66	     `--pin-freq` run carries it and droops anyway.

68	     set, and say on the report that a descent's numbers are

# Known bugs

This file uses [Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form). It
lists known defects we're aware of but haven't scheduled a fix for.
Each entry describes what goes wrong, when, and the cost of
the failure. Entries are numbered (`1.` `2.` ...) the same way
as `## Todo` in `../TODO.md`. Run
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/bugs.md` to renumber after
insert / delete / reorder.

## Bugs

1. 2t benches accept a 1-CPU pin pool and livelock through spin
   handoffs. `core_for` wraps the pin pool (`src/harness.rs`),
   so e.g. `iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-2t --pin 8` pins both the main
   thread and the spinning echo worker to core 8. Neither side
   yields, so every handoff waits for an involuntary preemption
   (milliseconds instead of ~200 ns), and the 5×1,000-step cost
   estimate alone takes minutes and the run appears hung.
   Observed on 3900x 2026-07-26, and `--pin 8,9` behaves normally.
   Cost: an apparent hang the user must ^C, with no hint that
   the pinning was the cause. The bug requires pinning: an
   unpinned run lets the scheduler separate the threads and
   behaves normally. Fix direction:
   - Track `core_for` requests in `RunCfg` (max `thread_idx`
     asked for): thread placement only goes through `core_for`
     when pinning is active, so refusing a pool with fewer
     unique CPUs than requested placements covers every path
     to this bug, with no per-bench thread-count declaration
     needed.
   - Independently, put a wall-clock deadline on the open-loop
     5×1,000-step estimate phase so *any* pathologically slow
     bench aborts with a diagnostic instead of hanging.
   - Update 2026-08-02 (0.24.0): the deadline half is fixed structurally: the estimate phase is
     gone, and every warmup pass is deadlined by the warm cap (`--warm-cap`, default 1.5 s), so
     the hang shrinks to a bounded wait ending in an "uncertified" report. The pool-size guard
     half remains open (the run still livelocks through the measurement itself).
   - Update 2026-09-02 (0.27.0): `cb-seg-2t` joins the spinning 2t set this covers. `cb-chan-2t`
     parks and does not.

2. `suggest-freq` perturbs the run it measures. Its descent
   wraps each candidate's bench in `sample_while`
   (`src/freqctl.rs:699`), which spawns an unpinned thread
   that wakes about 20 times a second to read
   `scaling_cur_freq`. An ordinary run has no such thread.
   Measured on 7600x 2026-09-04 with `zcr-mpsc-2t
   --blocks=100 --inner 100 -d 60 --pin-cpus 1,2`, three
   interleaved reps per arm, every run graded A:
   `--pin-freq=4701` read 74.43 / 74.15 / 74.41 ns while
   `suggest-freq` at that same 4701 read 62.51 / 62.82 /
   62.89, an 18.5% gap. Both reported `4.67->4.67GHz 99%`
   and both verified "Delivered 4.66-4.67 GHz". The gap is
   real work rather than a display artifact: `outer` was
   7.93M against 9.40M in the same 60.8 s, a ratio of 1.185
   matching the latency ratio exactly. We think the waker
   holds the package out of deep idle and the fabric clock
   with it, which is what a cross-core round trip rides.
   Cost: a `suggest-freq` bench report cannot be compared
   against any ordinary run's, and nothing on the report
   says so. Fix direction:
   - Reuse the run's own delivered-clock series instead of
     sampling separately. Every run already records one
     (`clock_t_ns` / `clock_cpu` / `clock_khz` in the
     record, and the settle cell is built from it), and that
     path demonstrably does not perturb, since the plain
     `--pin-freq` run carries it and droops anyway.
   - Failing that, pin the sampler outside the bench's CPU
     set, and say on the report that a descent's numbers are
     measured under a sampler.
   - Sampling inline on the measuring thread works only at
     block granularity. `outer` runs to millions, so a
     per-sample sysfs read would cost more than it measures,
     while the block gap is already a non-measuring window.
   - Whichever way it lands, the fixed `suggest-freq` will
     report *slower* numbers than it does today, which is
     correct: it should measure what an ordinary run gets.

# References

321	## Comparing implementations: least significant change
322	
323	How to decide whether implementation A is really faster than B
324	at 95% confidence, worked from a six-run tp-pc series on
325	r5-7600x (2026-07-13).
326	
327	The unit of replication is the **run**, not the sample. A run's
328	millions of samples make its within-run standard error
329	microscopic; what dominates comparison error is run-to-run
330	systematic drift (mode mix, frequency regime, calibration).
331	So compare per-run statistics:
332	
333	- Do n runs of A and n of B — n is the **replication count per
334	  implementation** (n=5 → 10 runs total) — **interleaved**
335	  (A,B,A,B,...) so thermal / frequency drift hits both arms
336	  alike; same machine, same duration, same pinning; discard an
337	  initial warm-up run.
338	- Take one statistic per run (today `mean min-p99`; the
339	  trimmed p10-p90 row when it lands), giving n values per arm.
340	- Two-sample t at 95%: LSC = t(0.975, 2n-2) * s * sqrt(2/n),
341	  with s the pooled run-to-run stdev of the statistic.
342	
343	From the observed series (`mean min-p99`: 4752.5, 4852.1,
344	4763.7, 4834.0, 4726.6, 4863.2 ns → s ≈ 58 ns ≈ 1.2%):
345	
346	- n=3 → LSC ≈ 131 ns (~2.7%)
347	- n=5 → LSC ≈ 85 ns (~1.8%)
348	- n=10 → LSC ≈ 55 ns (~1.1%)
349	
350	Choosing n: invert the formula for the difference Δ you need
351	to resolve — n ≈ 2 * (t * s / Δ)². At s ≈ 1.2%: Δ=2% → n≈5,
352	Δ=1% → n≈10-12, Δ=0.5% → n≈40. n=5 is the practical default.
353	
354	A single run cannot yield an honest LSC: between-run variance
355	is invisible from inside one run, and a run's internal error
356	bar (stdev/sqrt(samples) ≈ 0.4 ns here) understates the true
357	run-to-run spread (~58 ns) by two orders of magnitude. Longer
358	runs don't substitute for more runs — the -d {5..100} series'
359	means wobble as much at 100 s as at 5 s, because the dominant
360	variance is per-invocation systematic state (thread placement,
361	frequency regime, mode mix): a longer run averages longer over
362	the *same* draw; only re-running re-rolls it.
363	
364	### Within-invocation replication: sleep-separated blocks
365	
366	Idea (2026-07-13 session): chop one invocation into Y blocks
367	separated by an OS sleep of random ms length, compute the
368	per-block statistic, and use Y as the replication count in the
369	LSC formula (df = 2Y-2) — an LSC from a single invocation.
370	The spin dither handles sub-quantum phase; the sleeps target
371	the bigger per-invocation state:
372	
373	- **Mode mix re-rolls** — we think the closed-loop mode mix is
374	  a semi-stable attractor (why it shows up as *between*-run
375	  variance); a sleep by one thread breaks the rhythm and
376	  re-rolls the attractor, converting the dominant hidden
377	  variance into something blocks can observe.
378	- **Thread placement re-rolls only weakly** — wake affinity
379	  returns a thread to its cache-hot core on an idle box; moot
380	  under pinning.
381	- **Not re-rolled**: process-start state (memory layout/ASLR,
382	  the calibration draw — cached constants fix that anyway), so
383	  block variance may understate invocation variance.
384	- Mechanics: discard a short post-wake warm-up per block (each
385	  wake pays a frequency ramp + cache refill — the measured
386	  cold-calibration effect); randomize sleep length so block
387	  boundaries don't phase-lock with kernel ticks or workload
388	  periodicity.
389	- **Validation required** before trusting the single-run LSC:
390	  ~10 invocations x Y=10 blocks, compare between-block vs
391	  between-invocation variance (ANOVA). Close → honest; short →
392	  report must say so.
393	- Payoff: block-wise **A/B interleaving** in one invocation

396	  ambient load) and tightens the LSC beyond unpaired runs;
397	  same reason hyperfine alternates commands. Would largely

399

## Comparing implementations: least significant change

How to decide whether implementation A is really faster than B
at 95% confidence, worked from a six-run tp-pc series on
r5-7600x (2026-07-13).

The unit of replication is the **run**, not the sample. A run's
millions of samples make its within-run standard error
microscopic; what dominates comparison error is run-to-run
systematic drift (mode mix, frequency regime, calibration).
So compare per-run statistics:

- Do n runs of A and n of B — n is the **replication count per
  implementation** (n=5 → 10 runs total) — **interleaved**
  (A,B,A,B,...) so thermal / frequency drift hits both arms
  alike; same machine, same duration, same pinning; discard an
  initial warm-up run.
- Take one statistic per run (today `mean min-p99`; the
  trimmed p10-p90 row when it lands), giving n values per arm.
- Two-sample t at 95%: LSC = t(0.975, 2n-2) * s * sqrt(2/n),
  with s the pooled run-to-run stdev of the statistic.

From the observed series (`mean min-p99`: 4752.5, 4852.1,
4763.7, 4834.0, 4726.6, 4863.2 ns → s ≈ 58 ns ≈ 1.2%):

- n=3 → LSC ≈ 131 ns (~2.7%)
- n=5 → LSC ≈ 85 ns (~1.8%)
- n=10 → LSC ≈ 55 ns (~1.1%)

Choosing n: invert the formula for the difference Δ you need
to resolve — n ≈ 2 * (t * s / Δ)². At s ≈ 1.2%: Δ=2% → n≈5,
Δ=1% → n≈10-12, Δ=0.5% → n≈40. n=5 is the practical default.

A single run cannot yield an honest LSC: between-run variance
is invisible from inside one run, and a run's internal error
bar (stdev/sqrt(samples) ≈ 0.4 ns here) understates the true
run-to-run spread (~58 ns) by two orders of magnitude. Longer
runs don't substitute for more runs — the -d {5..100} series'
means wobble as much at 100 s as at 5 s, because the dominant
variance is per-invocation systematic state (thread placement,
frequency regime, mode mix): a longer run averages longer over
the *same* draw; only re-running re-rolls it.

### Within-invocation replication: sleep-separated blocks

Idea (2026-07-13 session): chop one invocation into Y blocks
separated by an OS sleep of random ms length, compute the
per-block statistic, and use Y as the replication count in the
LSC formula (df = 2Y-2) — an LSC from a single invocation.
The spin dither handles sub-quantum phase; the sleeps target
the bigger per-invocation state:

- **Mode mix re-rolls** — we think the closed-loop mode mix is
  a semi-stable attractor (why it shows up as *between*-run
  variance); a sleep by one thread breaks the rhythm and
  re-rolls the attractor, converting the dominant hidden
  variance into something blocks can observe.
- **Thread placement re-rolls only weakly** — wake affinity
  returns a thread to its cache-hot core on an idle box; moot
  under pinning.
- **Not re-rolled**: process-start state (memory layout/ASLR,
  the calibration draw — cached constants fix that anyway), so
  block variance may understate invocation variance.
- Mechanics: discard a short post-wake warm-up per block (each
  wake pays a frequency ramp + cache refill — the measured
  cold-calibration effect); randomize sleep length so block
  boundaries don't phase-lock with kernel ticks or workload
  periodicity.
- **Validation required** before trusting the single-run LSC:
  ~10 invocations x Y=10 blocks, compare between-block vs
  between-invocation variance (ANOVA). Close → honest; short →
  report must say so.
- Payoff: block-wise **A/B interleaving** in one invocation
  (A,B,A,B with sleeps between) analyzed as *paired* block
  differences — pairing cancels common-mode drift (thermal,
  ambient load) and tightens the LSC beyond unpaired runs;
  same reason hyperfine alternates commands. Would largely
  subsume a plain `--runs n` mode.

Reducing s beats raising n (LSC shrinks only as 1/sqrt(n)):

- A statistic that ignores the mode-mix wobble — the p10-p90
  trimmed mean's observed run-to-run spread was ~±0.2%, putting
  a 5-run LSC near 0.4%.
- A pinned frequency regime (`performance` governor on the
  bench box) and cached calibration constants (this cycle)
  remove two more run-to-run variables.
- A headless idle machine: r5-7600x repeats warm calibration
  constants to ±0.02%; the desktop 3900X wobbles ~±5%.

553	### Block validation results (0.21.0-4, r5-7600x)
554	
555	`mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 10`, checking whether the single-run
556	block CI predicts between-invocation spread:
557	
558	- **Unpinned, 8 invocations**: invocation means are bimodal —
559	  a fast tight state (4,885-4,948 ns, CIs ±19-38) and a slow
560	  loose one (5,048-5,252 ns, CIs ±97-189). Between-invocation
561	  s ≈ 124 ns vs a blocks-predicted ≈ 52 ns: blocks captured
562	  only ~20% of the between-invocation variance. We think the
563	  missing component is thread placement — it persists for the
564	  process lifetime, so 1-10 ms sleeps never re-roll it.
565	- **Pinned (`--pin 0,1`), 6 invocations**: means 4,713-4,795,
566	  s ≈ 29 ns (0.6%), bimodality gone; single-run CIs 7.5-48 ns
567	  (LSC 10-63 ns, 0.2-1.3%). Residual between-invocation state
568	  is still ~4× the block-sampling prediction, but small in
569	  absolute terms.
570	- **No blocked-vs-unblocked shift**: three unblocked pinned
571	  runs' trimmed means (4,709-4,732) sit inside the blocked
572	  range — the sleeps + post-wake warm-ups don't move the
573	  measurement.
574	
575	Interpretation: the report's `CI95` / `LSC` lines are honest
576	*within-invocation* replication — use them as a lower bound on
577	cross-invocation confidence, pin to remove the placement state
578	(unpinned it dominates), and keep interleaved multi-run
579	comparison for final A/B calls.
580	
581	### Merged block validation results (0.28.11-7, 3900X)
582	
583	The grade signals, the resolution curve, and the default block count were tuned on 0.05 s batches.
584	The `feat: merge batches into blocks` cycle made the block the one unit, so the shapes above were
585	rerun on it on the 3900X (2026-09-12, powersave with `balance_performance`, unpinned unless
586	named). Records are unfiled in the ignored `tmp/blockval-20260912/`.
587	
588	- **The grades hold on the merged unit.** `min-now -d 5` at 10 and 100 sleepless blocks, three
589	  interleaved runs each: still runs read A at both counts. The box's bistable floor, 22.1-22.5 ns
590	  against 24-27 ns, read F where it moved inside a run, and A where a whole run sat in the slow
591	  state (27.1 ns, graded A). The letters track movement within a run, not the level, as designed.
592	- **Short blocks raise no false alarm.** `min-now -d 1 --blocks 100` makes 10 ms blocks of about
593	  18,000 samples, and a still run read drift and step 0.00% A. `mpsc-2t -d 3 --blocks 100
594	  --pin-cpus 0,1` makes blocks of about 4,800 samples and read A on a still run.
595	- **The count is what lets resolution see drift.** At 10 blocks the curve has one level, since a
596	  second needs [`MIN_GROUPS`](../src/resolution.rs) groups, so `resolution` equals `LSC` exactly.
597	  At 100 blocks it has several, and a drifting run reads above LSC: 136 against 84 ns, and 4,481
598	  against 1,567 ns, on the pinned `mpsc-2t -d 10` series.
599	- **The merge moved no number.** `mpsc-2t -d 3 --pin-cpus 0,1`, the plain 0.28.10 and the dev
600	  build interleaved, four runs each: means 6,433-7,722 ns plain and 6,329-6,463 ns dev, grades
601	  A to D and A to C.
602	- **This box's config costs what was predicted.** `min-now -d 5` with the 1-10 ms sleep ran
603	  5.2-5.3 s at 10 blocks and 5.9-6.0 s at 100.
604	- **Count sizing does not bound the run.** A block runs a fixed sample count sized from the
605	  warmup's step cost, and that cost is the warmup's best pass. Where a bench has a fast state the
606	  best pass reads it, so the count is sized for a speed the run does not keep:
607	
608	  | run                                  | sized cost | measured mean | duration |
609	  |--------------------------------------|-----------:|--------------:|---------:|
610	  | `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, typical       |   2,962 ns |      6,367 ns |    6.6 s |
611	  | `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, fast warmup   |     573 ns |      6,463 ns |   34.2 s |
612	  | `mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 100`, worst  |   1,973 ns |     14,047 ns |   72.3 s |
613	
614	  The plain 0.28.10 bounded every block by time and held 3.08 s on each of its four runs.
615	  `min-now`, whose best pass is its mean, ran within 10% of its budget throughout.
616	
617	Verdict: 100 blocks stands as the default, and the grades need no retuning for the merged unit.
618	Sizing the count from the warmup's best pass leaves a run's wall time unbounded, by 11x at worst
619	in this series, and wants a fix before the sleep default lands on top of it.
620	
621	The fix, in the same cycle: the count is sized from the median of the warmup's exit-window passes,
622	and a time-budgeted block stops at its count or at twice its share of the budget, whichever comes
623	first, with `mean` weighted by block sample counts so a cut block leaves it exact. Rerun with
624	this box's 100-block config, its 1-10 ms sleep included in every duration:
625	
626	| run                                     | plain 0.28.10 |     before fix | after fix |
627	|-----------------------------------------|--------------:|---------------:|----------:|
628	| `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, six runs         |     3.8-3.9 s |   6.5-34.2 s * | 3.8-4.9 s |
629	| `mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 100`, three runs |             - |    8.1-72.3 s  | 10.6-12.1 s |
630

### Block validation results (0.21.0-4, r5-7600x)

`mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 10`, checking whether the single-run
block CI predicts between-invocation spread:

- **Unpinned, 8 invocations**: invocation means are bimodal —
  a fast tight state (4,885-4,948 ns, CIs ±19-38) and a slow
  loose one (5,048-5,252 ns, CIs ±97-189). Between-invocation
  s ≈ 124 ns vs a blocks-predicted ≈ 52 ns: blocks captured
  only ~20% of the between-invocation variance. We think the
  missing component is thread placement — it persists for the
  process lifetime, so 1-10 ms sleeps never re-roll it.
- **Pinned (`--pin 0,1`), 6 invocations**: means 4,713-4,795,
  s ≈ 29 ns (0.6%), bimodality gone; single-run CIs 7.5-48 ns
  (LSC 10-63 ns, 0.2-1.3%). Residual between-invocation state
  is still ~4× the block-sampling prediction, but small in
  absolute terms.
- **No blocked-vs-unblocked shift**: three unblocked pinned
  runs' trimmed means (4,709-4,732) sit inside the blocked
  range — the sleeps + post-wake warm-ups don't move the
  measurement.

Interpretation: the report's `CI95` / `LSC` lines are honest
*within-invocation* replication — use them as a lower bound on
cross-invocation confidence, pin to remove the placement state
(unpinned it dominates), and keep interleaved multi-run
comparison for final A/B calls.

### Merged block validation results (0.28.11-7, 3900X)

The grade signals, the resolution curve, and the default block count were tuned on 0.05 s batches.
The `feat: merge batches into blocks` cycle made the block the one unit, so the shapes above were
rerun on it on the 3900X (2026-09-12, powersave with `balance_performance`, unpinned unless
named). Records are unfiled in the ignored `tmp/blockval-20260912/`.

- **The grades hold on the merged unit.** `min-now -d 5` at 10 and 100 sleepless blocks, three
  interleaved runs each: still runs read A at both counts. The box's bistable floor, 22.1-22.5 ns
  against 24-27 ns, read F where it moved inside a run, and A where a whole run sat in the slow
  state (27.1 ns, graded A). The letters track movement within a run, not the level, as designed.
- **Short blocks raise no false alarm.** `min-now -d 1 --blocks 100` makes 10 ms blocks of about
  18,000 samples, and a still run read drift and step 0.00% A. `mpsc-2t -d 3 --blocks 100
  --pin-cpus 0,1` makes blocks of about 4,800 samples and read A on a still run.
- **The count is what lets resolution see drift.** At 10 blocks the curve has one level, since a
  second needs [`MIN_GROUPS`](../src/resolution.rs) groups, so `resolution` equals `LSC` exactly.
  At 100 blocks it has several, and a drifting run reads above LSC: 136 against 84 ns, and 4,481
  against 1,567 ns, on the pinned `mpsc-2t -d 10` series.
- **The merge moved no number.** `mpsc-2t -d 3 --pin-cpus 0,1`, the plain 0.28.10 and the dev
  build interleaved, four runs each: means 6,433-7,722 ns plain and 6,329-6,463 ns dev, grades
  A to D and A to C.
- **This box's config costs what was predicted.** `min-now -d 5` with the 1-10 ms sleep ran
  5.2-5.3 s at 10 blocks and 5.9-6.0 s at 100.
- **Count sizing does not bound the run.** A block runs a fixed sample count sized from the
  warmup's step cost, and that cost is the warmup's best pass. Where a bench has a fast state the
  best pass reads it, so the count is sized for a speed the run does not keep:

  | run                                  | sized cost | measured mean | duration |
  |--------------------------------------|-----------:|--------------:|---------:|
  | `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, typical       |   2,962 ns |      6,367 ns |    6.6 s |
  | `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, fast warmup   |     573 ns |      6,463 ns |   34.2 s |
  | `mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 100`, worst  |   1,973 ns |     14,047 ns |   72.3 s |

  The plain 0.28.10 bounded every block by time and held 3.08 s on each of its four runs.
  `min-now`, whose best pass is its mean, ran within 10% of its budget throughout.

Verdict: 100 blocks stands as the default, and the grades need no retuning for the merged unit.
Sizing the count from the warmup's best pass leaves a run's wall time unbounded, by 11x at worst
in this series, and wants a fix before the sleep default lands on top of it.

The fix, in the same cycle: the count is sized from the median of the warmup's exit-window passes,
and a time-budgeted block stops at its count or at twice its share of the budget, whichever comes
first, with `mean` weighted by block sample counts so a cut block leaves it exact. Rerun with
this box's 100-block config, its 1-10 ms sleep included in every duration:

| run                                     | plain 0.28.10 |     before fix | after fix |
|-----------------------------------------|--------------:|---------------:|----------:|
| `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, six runs         |     3.8-3.9 s |   6.5-34.2 s * | 3.8-4.9 s |
| `mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 100`, three runs |             - |    8.1-72.3 s  | 10.6-12.1 s |

\* measured at the 10-block config, whose sleeps cost about 0.5 s less.

The cap cut one block in the three `-d 10` runs and none in `min-now`, so counts stay equal
wherever the median estimate holds, and the cap is the backstop for a bench that changes state
after its warmup.

### Analyze a directory of records

A record exists so a re-analysis can happen without the session that produced it, and nothing reads
one back, so every analysis is a throwaway script whose numbers nobody can check (wink, 2026-09-03,
reading the 7600X duration sweep). An `analyze` subcommand over a directory of records, sharing
`record.rs`'s struct so the schema keeps one owner.

- three tiers, in increasing order of what they are worth:
  - **tabulate**: pivot the records into a table on an axis, duration, host, bench, or run. The
    least interesting tier, and the one the other two are built on
  - **read the series nothing reads**: `block_mean_ns`, `block_samples`, `clock_t_ns`, `clock_cpu`,
    and `clock_khz` sit in every record and nothing reads them back, roughly a third of the file's
    bytes as dead weight. The drift and step signals are computed at run time and thrown away, and
    the record holds the raw material to recompute them
  - **make a cross-run claim**: the tool cannot make one at all today. Every number it prints is a
    within-invocation claim, and the guide already says so, treating `LSC` as a lower bound and
    telling the reader to run 3-5 interleaved and compare the per-run values by hand ([Comparing
    two implementations](docs/report-guide.md#comparing-two-implementations)). Nothing performs
    that comparison
- the cross-run tier is the entry's point: run-to-run scatter, a confidence interval on the mean of
  run means, and an `LSC` that is not fiction. Single-run resolution understates the real spread
  badly on the contended benches, `cb-chan-2t`'s 5 s and 30 s runs disagreeing by 10.9% while the
  5 s run claims 0.15% resolution, 64x its own claim
- one run per cell cannot say which of the two runs was the off one, so the sweep that found this
  was the wrong shape. 3-5 runs per cell, interleaved, is what the guide has said all along
- the output reuses the report's row names, so the guide decodes the new surface for free. Grading
  the set the way a run grades itself is the natural extension: do these runs agree, and is a
  disagreement drift, a step, or one bad run
- `--format csv` / `--format json` for the plotting hand-off, kin to "Machine-readable report
  output" below, one flag family
- its cross-run arithmetic is the spawning entry's, one statistics module serving both, and the
  records carry the host block cross-host analysis needs, a hostname alone naming nothing

## The measurement hierarchy

Every number in a report is computed at one of five levels.
Knowing which level a number lives at is most of reading it:

1. **Call**: one execution of the bench's operation (for
   `min-now`, one `Instant::now()`). Never timed individually.
2. **Sample**: the unit that is actually timed. One timer pair
   brackets `inner` back-to-back calls, and the reading divided
   by `inner` is the recorded per-call value (kept in
   picoseconds, so sub-ns precision survives). `inner` is
   auto-sized so the timer's own cost stays a small fraction of
   the workload's, and it sets the **quantum**, the smallest value
   step a sample can express.
3. **Block** (`--blocks N`): consecutive samples, with an
   optional sleep and unrecorded warmup in front, every block
   sized to one sample count from the warmup's typical step
   cost, and stopped early at twice its share of the budget
   when the bench runs slower than that (the report says how
   many). Blocks are the run's **time axis** and its
   **replication axis** at once. The grade block's drift, step,
   bursts, and interference signals, the delivered-clock
   series, and the `resolution` row are computed over the
   block series, and `mean` is its count-weighted average. The
   default `--block-sleep` of 1-10 ms makes each block a
   mini-run separated by a state-re-rolling sleep, and the
   spread of block means yields CI95 and LSC. Every run has
   blocks, 100 by default, so a five-second run's blocks are
   about 50 ms. With `--block-sleep 0`, blocks are partitions of one continuous run and CI95
   and LSC print `-`, and below eight blocks the stats that
   need more print `-` as well.
4. **Run**: one process invocation. Run-to-run scatter is
   *larger* than anything a single run can see, which is why the
   `resolution` row exists and why decisions that matter want
   3-5 interleaved runs.
5. **Series**: several runs, interleaved when comparing, a
   records directory and its tags. Nothing in a report is
   computed here yet: the comparison is the reader's, by the
   method in [Comparing two
   implementations](#comparing-two-implementations).

So: `calls = samples x inner`, the histogram's population is
`samples`, and blocks partition those samples in time, and
replicate the run when a sleep separates them.

363	## Comparing two implementations
364	
365	"Is B really faster than A, or is it noise?" The workflow:
366	
367	```
368	iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin-cpus 0,1 --blocks 10 --block-sleep 1-10ms --block-warmup 2ms -d 10
369	```
370	
371	`--blocks 10 -d 10` divides the 10-second measuring budget
372	into **10 blocks of ~1 s each**: same total measurement, now
373	with an error bar, because `--block-sleep` makes each block a
374	mini-run (its sleep draw re-rolls scheduler/frequency state,
375	`--block-warmup` keeps the post-wake ramp out of the samples,
376	then the block measures its share of the budget). The sleep
377	defaults to 1-10 ms and the warmup to 0. With `--block-sleep 0`
378	the blocks are partitions of one continuous run, and CI95/LSC
379	print `-` rather than a number built on replication that never
380	happened. Always pin
381	(`--pin-cpus`): unpinned, the OS's thread placement is re-rolled
382	per *process* and dominates run-to-run drift, which blocks
383	can't see. The report then ends with:
384	
385	```
386	  mean         4,745.953 ns
387	  ...
388	  resolution      12.41  ns
389	  CI95            16.115 ns
390	  LSC             21.169 ns
391	```
392	
393	- **mean**: the run's headline number: the mean of the 10 block
394	  means weighted by their sample counts, and so the exact mean
395	  of every sample.
396	- **resolution**: printed on **every** run: the block-curve
397	  drift floor, the smallest delta this run can honestly
398	  distinguish. Block means are aggregated in groups of 1, 2,
399	  4, ... and where their variance stops falling as `1/n` is
400	  drift the run cannot average away.
401	- **CI95**: 95% confidence interval (half-width) on that
402	  mean: "the true value is within ±16 ns of 4,746, as far as
403	  this run can tell."
404	- **LSC**: least significant change: run the *other*
405	  implementation the same way (same `-d`, same `--blocks`,
406	  same knobs, same pin), and if the two `mean` values differ
407	  by more than roughly the larger of the two `LSC`s, the
408	  difference is real at 95% confidence.

## Comparing two implementations

"Is B really faster than A, or is it noise?" The workflow:

```
iiac-perf mpsc-2t --pin-cpus 0,1 --blocks 10 --block-sleep 1-10ms --block-warmup 2ms -d 10
```

`--blocks 10 -d 10` divides the 10-second measuring budget
into **10 blocks of ~1 s each**: same total measurement, now
with an error bar, because `--block-sleep` makes each block a
mini-run (its sleep draw re-rolls scheduler/frequency state,
`--block-warmup` keeps the post-wake ramp out of the samples,
then the block measures its share of the budget). The sleep
defaults to 1-10 ms and the warmup to 0. With `--block-sleep 0`
the blocks are partitions of one continuous run, and CI95/LSC
print `-` rather than a number built on replication that never
happened. Always pin
(`--pin-cpus`): unpinned, the OS's thread placement is re-rolled
per *process* and dominates run-to-run drift, which blocks
can't see. The report then ends with:

```
  mean         4,745.953 ns
  ...
  resolution      12.41  ns
  CI95            16.115 ns
  LSC             21.169 ns
```

- **mean**: the run's headline number: the mean of the 10 block
  means weighted by their sample counts, and so the exact mean
  of every sample.
- **resolution**: printed on **every** run: the block-curve
  drift floor, the smallest delta this run can honestly
  distinguish. Block means are aggregated in groups of 1, 2,
  4, ... and where their variance stops falling as `1/n` is
  drift the run cannot average away.
- **CI95**: 95% confidence interval (half-width) on that
  mean: "the true value is within ±16 ns of 4,746, as far as
  this run can tell."
- **LSC**: least significant change: run the *other*
  implementation the same way (same `-d`, same `--blocks`,
  same knobs, same pin), and if the two `mean` values differ
  by more than roughly the larger of the two `LSC`s, the
  difference is real at 95% confidence.

Caveat: the block rows see *within-invocation* variation
only. Some per-process state survives even long sleeps
(measured ~0.6% residual drift even pinned, on an idle Ryzen
5 7600X), so treat `LSC` as a lower bound and `resolution` as
the honest single-run claim. For a decision that matters, run
each implementation 3-5 times interleaved (A,B,A,B,...) and

- **Messages:** nothing is waiting for us in `vc-x1-messages` and no session holds it. I haven't fetched new messages; say so if you want a fetch.

I'll clean up the continuation notes in the opening commit.

## Proposed cycle

**Title:** `feat: CI95 and LSC across processes`. The full entry title would make a very long bookmark name, but I can use it if you prefer.
- It's multi-step.
- Opening version: 0.28.14-0.
- The opening renames the package to `iiac-perf-dev`.

**Problem:** A process start re-rolls where the rings and stacks land in memory, and that placement sets a bench's level. So CI95 and LSC computed over blocks inside one process understate the real spread. The 7600x evidence shows it: runs claimed CI95 under 0.1 ns but landed on levels 60 to 76 ns.

**Solution:**
- Every bench in a list, including `all`, runs in its own child process.
- A bench can be repeated across N fresh processes. With a bench list, the order rotates through the list each round (A, B, A, B), which gives the interleaved A/B the guide recommends.
- CI95 and LSC are computed over the per-process means, using one statistics module that also serves the within-process numbers.

**Acceptance check**, on this host:
1. `iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v0-2t zcr-mpsc-v1-2t --runs 3 --pin-cpus 0,1 -d 2 --record <dir>`
2. The recorded pids are all different, and the timestamps alternate between the two benches.
3. Each bench prints its across-process mean, CI95 and LSC next to its within-process values, each labeled.
4. A unit test reproduces the design note's worked LSC numbers (for example n=3 gives about 131 ns).
5. `vc-x1 validate` passes.

**Ladder:**
1. `feat: CI95 and LSC across processes opening`
2. `refactor: one statistics owner for a series of means`: moves `t975`, the CI95 and LSC arithmetic out of `harness.rs`, and `resolution.rs`'s LSC formula into one module.
3. `feat: each bench runs in its own child process`
   - The parent starts sleep inhibit and pins the clock once. The pin undoes itself when dropped, so a child must not pin it or it would undo the parent's pin.
   - Children get `--no-inhibit` and a hidden flag that makes them run exactly one bench.
   - `--pin-cpus` is passed through, because CPU affinity doesn't carry over to a child.
   - The child sends its results back as a `record.rs` `Record` written to a temp file, so the record format stays the single definition.
4. `feat: replicate each bench across processes, interleaved`: adds `--runs N` with a matching `runs` config key.
5. `feat: label the within-process and across-process error bars`: the report rows, plus a series id in the record so one invocation's children group together.
6. `docs: runs across processes in the guide and usage`
7. `feat: CI95 and LSC across processes closing`

**Left out of scope, staying as Todo items:**
- The page-offset and huge-pages experiment that tries to explain the levels.
- The 7600x `all` re-record, which is operational work.
- The `analyze` subcommand, which will reuse the new statistics module later.
- Moving `qualify-environment` onto the new child runner.

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Default for `--runs`.** I recommend 1: a child per bench, but no repeats unless asked. A default of 3 would make `all` take three times as long.
2. **Output when N > 1.** I recommend that the parent captures each child's output and prints one line per run (pid, mean, within-process CI95, grade), then the across-process summary. `-v` would show every child's full report. With N = 1, output looks the same as today.

4. **Escape hatch.** Should there be an `--in-process` flag that keeps today's behavior of running all benches in one process? I lean yes, because it's cheap and handy for debugging.

aiTitle: One bench per process, CI95 and LSC across processes

content.text:
## Interleaving

You're right that grouping is enough for each bench's own CI95. Five fresh processes re-roll placement, so their means are independent draws, whatever order they run in.

The LSC is different. It's a comparison, and the order is what protects a comparison.
- **Grouped:** A's five runs go first, then B's. Anything that drifts over those minutes (temperature, frequency regime, a background job, this desktop's two alternating speed levels) lands on one side only.
- **The result is bias, not spread:** the gap between A and B moves, and neither bench's CI95 widens. The LSC can't catch it, because it assumes both sets of runs came from the same conditions.
- **Interleaved (A, B, A, B):** the same drift hits both benches, so it goes into both benches' spread, where CI95 and LSC can see it.
- **Scale:** a grouped `all` at 5 runs of 5 s spans more than 12 minutes. Its first and last benches are that far apart, and so are any two benches you compare from it.

Interleaving costs no extra processes. The only cost is display: a bench's summary can't print until its last run, which for `all` is near the end. The one-line-per-run output would still show progress.

**My recommendation:** interleave by default. If you want grouping available, add an ordering setting, but I'd leave it out until something needs it. It's your call, since it's your model of the tool.

## Cold vs hot

Agreed. `blocks`, `block_sleep`, and `block_warmup` go to every child unchanged, so they still control what happens inside one process.

## `--run-sleep` / `run_sleep`

Agreed, and it's a good addition. Some details:

- **Spelling:** config keys use underscores (`block_sleep`, `settle_time`, `pin_freq`), so the key would be `run_sleep` and the flag `--run-sleep`.
- **Same format as `block_sleep`:** a fixed time or a random range such as `1-3s`, parsed by the existing time-span parser. A range keeps run starts from lining up with anything periodic on the machine.
- **Default 0:** starting a process, calibrating ticks, and warming up already put a gap in front of each run. Anyone who wants a cold start sets a sleep explicitly.
- **A collision with `qualify-environment`:** that subcommand already has `--runs` (default 10) and `--gap` (default 0), which does the same job as `--run-sleep`. I'd merge them:
  - `--runs` becomes one shared flag, with a default of 5 for benches and 10 for `qualify-environment`
  - `--gap` becomes `--run-sleep` for both, and `--gap` is removed

  Since `qualify-environment` already spawns runs, it may be worth moving it onto the new child runner in this cycle rather than later. I'd still keep that move out of scope and settle only the shared flag names here.

If you agree, these land in the `feat: replicate each bench across processes, interleaved` rung. That rung would be renamed `feat: replicate each bench across processes` if you choose grouping. The bookmark push is still waiting for your go.

The plain version: grouping is fine for each bench's own error bar, but interleaving keeps slow drift from biasing an A-versus-B comparison, and it costs nothing but a later summary. `--run-sleep` is worth adding. It would replace `qualify-environment`'s `--gap`, and `--runs` would be shared between the two modes.

content.text:
"Independent" in the statistics means two things, and fresh processes give only one of them:

1. **Independent draws.** No run inherits another run's state. A fresh process gives this, because placement is re-rolled.
2. **Identically distributed.** Every run draws from the same distribution. A fresh process can't give this, because the machine the runs share changes over time.

Grouped order is fine for the first and exposed on the second. A worked case:

- **Setup:** A and B are the same code. The host's level shifts 1% partway through the invocation. The cause could be heat building up, a background job, or the 3900X's two speed states: `min-now` sat at 22.1-22.5 ns or at 24-27 ns, and a whole run could sit in the slow state.
- **Grouped:** A's five runs all land before the shift and read about 100. B's five all land after it and read about 101.
  - Each arm's own spread is small, so each CI95 is small, and honest for its own window.
  - The pooled LSC comes out small too, perhaps 0.3.
  - The means differ by 1.0, so the tool says B is slower. That's a false call, because the difference is the clock on the wall, not the code.
- **Interleaved:** A and B each have runs on both sides of the shift. Each arm's means spread from 100 to 101, so the spread gets wider, the means agree, and nothing is called.

So independence protects each bench's CI95 from carried-over state, and interleaving protects the comparison between benches from time. A drifting host doesn't break independence. What it breaks is the assumption that A and B were measured under the same conditions, and grouping lines the arms up with the drift.

On a host that holds still for the whole invocation, the two orders give the same numbers. Examples are the idle headless 7600x with a pinned clock, or a short list. Interleaving is insurance that costs no extra processes. The only price is that a bench's summary prints after the whole list's last round rather than right after its own runs. These hosts have drifted before: the 3900X's two speed states, and the 18% clock-state effect in bugs.md entry 2. That history is why I'd buy the insurance. The randomized `run_sleep` range covers the leftover case of drift that repeats in step with the rounds.

If you want each bench reported as soon as its own runs finish, grouped still works. Comparisons across the list would then carry the caveat above, and the guide should say so.

Noted: `--gap` merges into `--run-sleep`, in the replication rung.

content.text:
You're mostly not wrong, and for the main use case not at all.

**Where you're right:**
- **Tuning is one bench per invocation.** There's nothing to interleave with. The comparison is between this build and the last one, and an edit and a rebuild separate them. No ordering inside one invocation can touch that.
- **Comparing benches works the way you describe.** You read each bench's mean, stdev, CI95, and LSC and compare. If the host holds still, interleaving changes nothing, as you say.
- **It isn't a race.** The benches don't contend with each other, so interleaving has nothing to do there.

**Where the reasoning has a gap, and it's a small one:** interleaving was never about the benches affecting each other. It's about slow changes in the host itself over minutes: heat, a background job, the 3900X's two speed states.
- `run_sleep`, `block_sleep`, and `block_warmup` re-roll short-lived state, such as a wake, a cache refill, or a frequency ramp. They don't stop the host drifting over the length of the invocation.
- So when two benches are run minutes apart, their difference includes whatever the host did in those minutes, and neither bench's CI95 contains it.

**Why it doesn't matter much:** your main use case already has that exposure, and at a bigger scale. Before and after a tweak are an hour or a day apart, and no ordering inside one invocation reaches across that. The honest claim is the same either way: the across-run CI95 and LSC are real for the window the runs covered, and a comparison with another window also carries whatever the host did in between. That's a sentence for the guide, not a feature.

**Recommendation:** drop interleaving. Each bench's runs go back to back, and its summary prints right after them. The rung becomes `feat: replicate each bench across processes`, and it still carries `--runs` / `runs` (default 5) and `--run-sleep` / `run_sleep` with `--gap` merged in. If you ever want two binaries measured under the same conditions, alternating them would be a separate Todo entry.

If that suits you, I'll start the opening commit: move the Todo entry into In Progress, bump to 0.28.14-0, rename to `iiac-perf-dev`, and file the continuation notes.

The plain version: you're right that interleaving adds nothing for tuning, and for benches compared by their own error bars it only guards against the host drifting between them. The guide can state that caveat, so I'd drop interleaving.

### Leads are labels, unmarked

the sentence after it is complete without it:

```

  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.

  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard

  renumbering.

  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.

  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label

`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
