796	## Bugs
797	
798	_See [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)._
799	
800	## Closed
801	
802	The last cycle's finished record, moved here whole by its closing commit and deleted by the next
803	opening ([Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). Earlier cycles are in the landmark commit's
804	copy of this section, and the cycles before the rule in the frozen [notes/chores/](notes/chores)
805	and [notes/done.md](notes/done.md).
806	
807	### feat: config and setup
808	
809	#### Problem
810	
811	A run's parameters come from defaults, the XDG file, the project-local file, and flags, and the
812	report names neither every value nor where each came from, so two records cannot be checked for
813	matching parameters (wink, 2026-09-12). And a host is ready for iiac-perf only after hand work: its
814	`[freq]` declaration written with the clamp limits, and sudo for every `--pin-freq` and
815	`restore-freq` (wink, 2026-09-14). A missing limit is a live hazard, [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)'s
816	`restore-freq` entry: the 3900X has no XDG config, and its only declaration omits both limits.
817	
818	#### Solution
819	
820	A run says what configured it, a record carries it, a host is made ready by one command, and a
821	benchmark directory pins every run while every restore returns to the host's own steady state.
822	
823	- **`Config:` list**: after `Setup:`, the files loaded and every run parameter with its value and
824	  source, `(default)`, the file, or the flag, marked `same as default` when a source restates the
825	  built-in, a `freq` line naming the declared `[freq]` table and its file. `Setup:` kept only the
826	  facts about the box
827	- **the record's `config` object**: schema 6, `config.files` and `config.params` keyed by name as
828	  `{value, source, same_as_default}`, paths absolute. No content hashes, since the values say more
829	  and a hash moves with a comment
830	- **`[freq]` declarations checked**: every pin and restore refuses a table without `min_mhz` and
831	  `max_mhz`, checks both against the boosted ceiling and a fixed frequency list, and allows
832	  `min_mhz = max_mhz`. `read-freq --as-config` prints the limits from the live clamp
833	- **`setup`**: prints the `[freq]` declaration it would add to `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` from
834	  the live state and the udev rule and root script handing the user the cpufreq files and
835	  `/dev/cpu_dma_latency`. `--apply` writes the config and runs the script through one sudo, and
836	  `--uninstall` plans the rule's removal. It never overwrites a config, compares an existing
837	  declaration with the live state, checks what it writes, and refuses to run as root or with an
838	  unsafe `USER`
839	- **restores say where the clock went**: every restore prints the file its `[freq]` came from and
840	  what it set, read back once the writes settle, the signal path printing the declared values
841	- **`pin_freq`**: a run key pinning every run, a frequency or `pin_mhz`, `min_mhz`, or `max_mhz`,
842	  `"no"` in a file meaning no key and `--pin-freq=no` skipping a file's pin for one run. Every pin
843	  target must fit under the boost-off ceiling, and a permission failure names its fix on a second
844	  line
845	- **the example configs**: `iiac-perf.example.md` in the markdown carrier replaced the TOML sample,
846	  and `iiac-perf.md` is untracked and ignored, still on the 3900X's disk
847	
848	#### Acceptance check
849	
850	A run's report prints `Config:` naming every parameter's source, and a `--record` line is schema 6
851	with a `config` object. `restore-freq` with a declaration lacking the clamp limits refuses and names
852	`setup`. `iiac-perf setup` on this host prints the config and the udev rule, `--apply` writes the
853	config and installs the rule, and afterwards `pin-freq` and `restore-freq` run without sudo on the
854	3900X and the 7600x, wink running the applies. `vc-x1 validate` passes.
855	
856	Passed, 2026-09-15, the host clauses run by wink:
857	
858	- a report prints `Config:` with every source, and a `--record` line is schema 6 with
859	  `config.files` and `config.params`
860	- `restore-freq` with a limit-less `[freq]` refused and named `setup`
861	- `setup` printed the config and the rule. `setup --apply` wrote the config and installed the rule
862	  on the 3900X, and on the 7600x the config was regenerated by `--apply` and the rule installed by
863	  wink
864	- without sudo, `--pin-freq` pinned and restored on both hosts, the 7600x after a reboot too, so the
865	  rule re-applies ownership at boot. The pin and restore ran through `--pin-freq`'s guard, the same
866	  writes the `pin-freq` and `restore-freq` command words make, which were not run sudo-free
867	- `vc-x1 validate` passed
868	
869	#### Ladder
870	
871	- [feat: config and setup opening][1] (done)
872	- [feat: a Config: list naming each value's source][2] (done)
873	- [feat: the record carries the run's config][3] (done)
874	- [fix: restore-freq refuses a declaration without clamp limits][4] (done)
875	- [feat: setup writes the host's freq declaration][5] (done)
876	- [feat: setup installs and removes the udev permissions][6] (done)
877	- [docs: one example config in the md carrier][7] (done)
878	- [fix: setup checks a declared [freq] against the live state][9] (done)
879	- [feat: say where the clock was restored to][10] (done)
880	- [feat: pin_freq as a config key][11] (done)
881	- [feat: config and setup closing][8] (done)
882	
883	#### Deliberation
884	
885	- **Config and setup in one cycle, ahead of spawning**: wink's ranking at `docs: file the
886	  continuation notes into their homes`.
887	  - spawning's parent checks the children's recorded config, its across-process error bars refuse
888	    mismatched parameters, and pinned children need `--pin-freq` without sudo
889	  - the halves share `config.rs` and `docs/config.md`, and setup writes the file the list names
890	- **`--config PATH` and key parity deferred**: split into their own Todo entry at the opening,
891	  since spawning can pass flags on the command line, keeping this ladder bounded.
892	- **`restore-freq` refuses rather than guesses**: a declared steady state, never a remembered one,
893	  is the `[freq]` table's standing rule, so missing limits are an error naming the fix.
894	- **No content hashes**: wink's call at the record rung, replacing the opening's plan to hash the
895	  loaded files.
896	  - every way a file shapes a run is already recorded as a value: the run keys in `config.params`,
897	    a profile's expansion in `pin_cpus`, and the live clock policy in the record's policy keys
898	  - a hash moves when a comment is edited and the run does not, so it adds only false mismatches
899	  - the one gap, a bare `--pin-freq` recording `on`, is closed by recording the resolved target
900	- **The remaining rungs under a waiver**: wink, at the restore-freq rung's push, delegated the
901	  rest of the cycle through the closing and the trapezoid pushed on the bookmark.
902	  - covers the work reviews, the description reviews, and every push to `feat-config-and-setup`,
903	    the trapezoid's included
904	  - does not cover Land: `main` is not moved, the plain name is not installed, and the bookmark
905	    stays
906	  - does not cover writes to a host: no `--apply`, no sudo, and no config written outside `tmp/`
907	- **Three rungs inserted after the trapezoid's push**: at wink's direction, reviewing the pushed
908	  cycle on real hosts, since the bookmark had not landed.
909	  - `fix: setup checks a declared [freq] against the live state`, when the 7600x's config held the
910	    3900X's clamp and `setup` passed it
911	  - `feat: say where the clock was restored to`, since which `[freq]` a restore uses depends on the
912	    directory, and its read-back found the settle and boosted-ceiling bugs
913	  - `feat: pin_freq as a config key`, a benchmark directory's pin as a run key, not a `[freq]`
914	    precedence trick, which resolved the "Two-regime runs" Todo entry
915	- **Host applies are wink's**: the sandbox cannot write `~/.config`, run sudo, or install a udev
916	  rule, so the setup rungs test the generated text and wink runs `--apply` on both hosts.
917	
918	#### Ladder details
919	
920	##### feat: config and setup opening
921	
922	The cycle's setup commit: publish the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, move the Todo entry
923	here and split its deferred half into its own entry, bump to the opening's version, and rename the
924	package to `iiac-perf-dev`.
925	
926	##### feat: a Config: list naming each value's source
927	
928	The report names some parameters and none of their sources, so a reader cannot tell a default from
929	a file's value from a flag. A `Config:` list after `Setup:` names each.
930	
931	- the loader records which file set each scalar key, the last overlay winning, so a source is known
932	  per key rather than per merged config
933	- one resolver, flag then file then default, returns every layered value with its source, and the
934	  `Config:` list is seventeen parameters: the eight config keys plus `samples`, `inner`, `pin_cpus`,
935	  `pin_freq`, `env_probe`, `ticks`, `inhibit`, `record`, and `tag`. `verbose` is left out, since it
936	  shapes logging and not the measurement
937	- names are the config keys' spelling, so the list, the file, and the coming record's `config`
938	  object share one vocabulary
939	- `same as default` compares rendered values, so `1-10 ms` in a file matches the built-in however
940	  the file spelled it
941	- `-D` shows the per-bench share with `--total-duration T over N benches` as its source, and a
942	  profile name shows its expansion, `smt = 0,12`
943	- `Setup:` keeps provenance about the box, the policy, the pins, and the inhibit state, and loses
944	  the block, warm-budget, and config-file lines to the list. The guide's quoted example outputs are
945	  historical and stay as they were
946	
947	##### feat: the record carries the run's config
948	
949	A record cannot be checked against another for matching parameters. Schema 6 adds a `config` object,
950	value and source per parameter, and the loaded files' paths.
951	
952	- `config.params` is the `Config:` list keyed by name, each `{value, source, same_as_default}`,
953	  rendered as the report prints it, so the report and the record read alike. The numeric keys
954	  (`blocks`, `block_sleep_min_s`, ...) stay, so an analysis never parses `1-10 ms`
955	- `config.files` and a file source are absolute paths, since the project-local file loads relative
956	  to a directory the record does not otherwise name
957	- `pin_freq` records the resolved target and where it came from, `3801 MHz (base clock ...)`,
958	  where the list had printed `on` for a bare `--pin-freq`, so a record says what clock the run held
959	- the recorder is built after the list resolves, still before any bench runs, so a bad `--record`
960	  path fails as fast as before
961	- the host, the tags, and the config travel together as the recorder's per-process stamp, which
962	  keeps the record builder's argument list inside clippy's limit
963	
964	##### fix: restore-freq refuses a declaration without clamp limits
965	
966	A declaration without `min_mhz` and `max_mhz` restores to the hardware range. Refuse it and name
967	`setup`.
968	
969	- the check sits in the steady-state resolver, so `restore-freq`, `pin-freq`, `--pin-freq`, and
970	  `suggest-freq` all refuse before any write, a pin needing its way home as much as a restore does
971	- the steady state's clamps are plain values now, so the restore plan has no hardware-range
972	  fallback left to reach
973	- the file still parses without the limits, the check living at use time like `epp` and `boost`,
974	  so a config that never pins is not broken by it
975	- `read-freq --as-config` printed the limits as an omitted comment, which the refusal would then
976	  reject, so it prints them from the live clamp in this rung, and comments them out when the clamp
977	  is pinned, since pasting a pin's `min = max` would make every restore a pin
978	- the refusal names `read-freq --as-config`, not `setup`, which does not exist until the next rung
979	  and joins the message there
980	
981	##### feat: setup writes the host's freq declaration
982	
983	A host's declaration is written by hand, and the hand forgets the limits. `setup` writes it from the
984	live state, clamp included.
985	
986	- print by default and write with `--apply`, so the file is read before it exists
987	- never overwrite, where the opening planned an overwrite flag: a missing file is created, a file
988	  without `[freq]` gains the section at its end, and a file declaring `[freq]` is left alone and
989	  checked, since an XDG config may hold profiles and knobs a regenerated file would lose. The
990	  flag has nothing left to guard, so it does not exist
991	- the new text is parsed and passed through the same steady-state checks every pin and restore
992	  applies before anything is written, so a clamp pinned at setup time refuses instead of writing a
993	  pin as the steady state
994	- the `[freq]` lines come from the one builder `read-freq --as-config` prints, so the two cannot
995	  disagree, and both refusal messages now name `setup` first
996	- `setup` refuses to run as root, since under sudo `$HOME` may be root's and the file would land in
997	  the wrong home
998	- testing here: print-only against the real home, and `--apply` against a scratch
999	  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` under the ignored `tmp/`, appending to a file with `blocks` and rechecking. The
1000	  real `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` is wink's to write, the sandbox's `~/.config` being
1001	  read-only
1002	
1003	##### feat: setup installs and removes the udev permissions
1004	
1005	Every pin and restore needs sudo. A udev rule granting the user ACLs on the cpufreq files and
1006	`/dev/cpu_dma_latency` removes that, installed and removed by `setup`.
1007	
1008	- ownership, not an ACL: the rule `chown`s each file to the user, since we think sysfs's POSIX ACL
1009	  support is not reliable, while `chown` on sysfs files is ordinary udev practice. Unverified here,
1010	  the sandbox's sysfs reading as `nobody`
1011	- the rule is one `RUN` per knob on each CPU's `add` event, plus the global boost on `cpu0` and an
1012	  `OWNER` on the latency device, so no shell quoting passes through udev and a knob a box lacks
1013	  fails only its own line. It carries no `$`, which udev would expand
1014	- the rule acts on boot and hotplug only, so `--apply` also takes ownership now, in one
1015	  `sudo sh -c` script that writes the rule, reloads udev, and `chown`s. The script names each
1016	  per-CPU knob once as a `cpu[0-9]*` glob, a 24-CPU box's 121 files reading as six lines
1017	- print first everywhere: `setup` shows the root script, `--apply` runs it, `--uninstall` shows the
1018	  removal, and `--uninstall --apply` removes the rule and gives the files back to root, leaving
1019	  the config alone
1020	- `USER` goes into the rule and the root script unquoted, so `setup` refuses a name that is not
1021	  letters, digits, `_`, `.`, and `-`
1022	- `setup` reports nothing to do when the rule file matches and the user owns every file, so a
1023	  second `--apply` asks for no password
1024	- the file list is the one the pin and restore plans write, exposed from `freqctl`, so the grant
1025	  cannot drift from what the commands need. The `apply` hint and the help text now name setup's
1026	  permissions beside root
1027	- untested here: the sandbox cannot run sudo or write `/etc`, so the rule and scripts are checked
1028	  as text, and wink's `--apply` on both hosts is the first real run
1029	
1030	##### docs: one example config in the md carrier
1031	
1032	Two example configs and a checked-in project-local config disagree about the recommended carrier
1033	and what a host declares. One `.md` example remains, and `iiac-perf.md` leaves git.
1034	
1035	- `iiac-perf.example.md` replaces `iiac-perf.toml.example`: every key at its built-in default,
1036	  each section's prose explaining its keys above the fence, and a commented `[freq]` pointing at
1037	  `setup` rather than values to copy. A test parses it and checks the defaults, so the sample
1038	  cannot drift from the loader
1039	- `iiac-perf.md` is untracked and ignored, not deleted: the opening held its removal until the
1040	  3900X's XDG config existed, and untracking keeps the file on that host's disk, so the host keeps
1041	  the declaration it had while the repo stops carrying one host's settings
1042	- finding: a project-local `[freq]` replaces the XDG one whole, so the untracked file's limit-less
1043	  table would shadow what `setup --apply` writes, for runs in the repo directory. Filed as the
1044	  Todo entry `setup warns when a project-local [freq] shadows the XDG one`, and in `notes/bugs.md`
1045	- the README no longer credits the local file with the hundred blocks, the default having carried
1046	  them since the merge-batches cycle
1047	
1048	##### fix: setup checks a declared [freq] against the live state
1049	
1050	Inserted after the trapezoid's push, at wink's direction, when the 7600x's `config.md` turned out to
1051	hold the 3900X's clamp, 1745-4673 MHz against its live 2991-5457. `setup` passed it, since both
1052	numbers fit the hardware range, so a restore there would cap the clock at 4.67 GHz. `setup` checks
1053	a declaration against the live state, and the notes that recorded the wrong values are corrected.
1054	
1055	- the comparison is the live state of the first CPU, the one `setup` declares from, and it covers
1056	  every declared value: governor, EPP, boost, and both limits. A declared `min_mhz = max_mhz` is a
1057	  legitimate steady state (wink, at this rung's review, pinning a benchmark host by config), so a
1058	  live pin at the same value and boost matches it, and a live pin against a declared range names
1059	  every difference with a note that a pin may still be running
1060	- a mismatch fails `setup`, naming each value and printing the live section, and never rewrites
1061	  the file: the fix is removing the table and rerunning `--apply`, or a `restore-freq` when the
1062	  declaration is the intended state
1063	- the steady-state check now holds `min_mhz` and `max_mhz` to a fixed-list driver's frequencies,
1064	  as `pin_mhz` already was, so every clamp value a restore writes is one the driver lists. The
1065	  other illegal values were refused already: zero and `min_mhz > max_mhz` at load, anything outside
1066	  the hardware range at use
1067	- the per-directory benchmark pin wink raised at the review, a project-local `[freq]` pin that
1068	  would also decide where a restore returns, becomes a run key in a later rung of this cycle,
1069	  `feat: pin_freq as a config key`, not a `[freq]` precedence trick
1070	- run on the 7600x as a copy in `/tmp`: it named `min_mhz` 1745 against 2991 and `max_mhz` 4673
1071	  against 5457. At wink's go the wrong file moved to `~/iiac-perf-data/` and `setup --apply` wrote
1072	  the live state, after which `setup` reported the declaration matching. The permissions step
1073	  failed at sudo, which needed a terminal, so no rule was installed and the files stayed root's
1074	- the prose `setup` writes above the fence named `restore-freq` beside the table as if it were a
1075	  key (wink, reading the new 7600x file). It now says the table is the steady state, that
1076	  `iiac-perf restore-freq` sets the governor, EPP, boost, and clamp to it, and that every pin
1077	  returns to it, and the 7600x's file was regenerated with that wording, its values unchanged
1078	- notes corrected: the ops notes and the `restore-freq` bug entry had recorded 2991 and 5457 on
1079	  2026-09-12, and the 3900X's record directories in `tmp/`, which the ops notes and three Todo
1080	  entries cite, were found gone the same day, so those citations now say so
1081	
1082	##### feat: say where the clock was restored to
1083	
1084	Inserted at wink's direction, at the live-state rung's review. A restore prints nothing, and which
1085	`[freq]` it used depends on the directory the run started in, so a user cannot tell where the clock
1086	went back to. Every restore says so: the state read back and the file its `[freq]` came from, the
1087	signal path printing the declared values it cannot read back. The `Config:` list and the record's
1088	`config.params` gain a `freq` line, the declared table and its file or `(none declared)`, since a
1089	`[freq]` set in a config showed nowhere in the report (wink, 2026-09-14, reading a run in the repo
1090	directory whose `iiac-perf.md` declared one).
1091	
1092	- one report after every restore's writes succeed: `freq: restored the [freq] from <file>:` and the
1093	  state lines read back from sysfs, so the line says what the CPU holds rather than what was asked.
1094	  `--pin-freq`'s guard, `suggest-freq`'s guard, and `restore-freq` share it, and `pin-freq` names
1095	  the file its later `restore-freq` would use from the same directory
1096	- the signal path prepares its line when the pin engages, the declared values and the file, and
1097	  writes it with a bare `write` after the restore, marked as declared and not read back, since a
1098	  handler may only write
1099	- the loader records the file that set `[freq]` under `freq` beside the scalar keys' sources, which
1100	  is what names the file in the report and in the `Config:` list
1101	- `Config:` gains `freq`, the table as one line or `none declared`, and the record's
1102	  `config.params` carries it the same way. A value past 24 characters no longer widens the value
1103	  column, so the one long line leaves every other line's source where it was
1104	- the read-back waits for the writes to land: wink's `sudo pin-freq` on the 3900X printed cpu0 at the
1105	  plan's 563 MHz staging floor and cpu1-23 at the old 1745 floor, while `read-freq` seconds later
1106	  showed 3801-3801 everywhere. The kernel applies amd-pstate limit changes after the write returns,
1107	  so every report now polls each written file every 10 ms, up to a second, until it reads back the
1108	  last token written, frequencies matching within 1 MHz, and says `not settled` naming the file
1109	  when one has not. `pin-freq`'s own lines wait the same way, and a pinned run and `suggest-freq`
1110	  wait silently before measuring, warning only when the pin has not landed
1111	- a pin in place broke the next pin: `--pin-freq` refused `max_mhz 4673` as outside `563-3801`,
1112	  because `cpuinfo_max_freq` reads the nominal frequency while boost is off. The declared limits are
1113	  now checked against the boosted ceiling, `amd_pstate_max_freq` where the driver exposes it, else
1114	  `cpuinfo_max_freq`, and a pin's target keeps the ceiling as it reads, since a pin turns boost off.
1115	  Without this, `restore-freq` itself would have refused to leave a pin once limits were declared
1116	- tested live on the 3900X by wink with the rung's first build: `sudo pin-freq` printed the
1117	  unsettled lines that led to the wait, and `--pin-freq` hit the ceiling bug. The settle and ceiling
1118	  logic are tested with a fake reader and a pinned-ceiling fixture. With the fixed build, wink's
1119	  `sudo iiac-perf-dev min-now -d 1 --pin-freq`, started while the box was still pinned, passed the
1120	  declared 4673 against the boosted ceiling, pinned at 3801, and ended with `freq: restored the
1121	  [freq] from iiac-perf.md:` over one settled state line, boost on and 1.75-4.67 GHz, which
1122	  `read-freq` then matched (2026-09-15). The Ctrl-C line is tested by its text only
1123	
1124	##### feat: pin_freq as a config key
1125	
1126	Inserted at wink's direction, at the same review. A benchmark directory can pin the clock only by
1127	declaring `min_mhz = max_mhz` in a project-local `[freq]`, which also moves where every restore
1128	returns. A `pin_freq` run key, the config twin of `--pin-freq`, pins every run and restores to the
1129	host's steady state on exit, a number for MHz or a word naming the host's value, and
1130	`--pin-freq=no` skips a config's pin for one run.
1131	
1132	- the values (wink, at this rung's review): a number for MHz, or a word naming the host's `[freq]`
1133	  value to pin at, `pin_mhz` (else the base clock, and the bare flag) or `min_mhz`, and `no` for no
1134	  pin. The same text works in the file and on the line, a quoted `"3801"` included. Booleans and
1135	  `on`/`off` were tried and dropped: `pin_freq` is which frequency, not a switch, and a word naming
1136	  the key says which. `max_mhz` is a word too (wink: if `min_mhz` is, `max_mhz` should be), pinning
1137	  whenever the declared value fits under the boost-off ceiling
1138	- every pin target is checked against the ceiling with boost off, which a pin turns off: the base
1139	  clock where the box has a boost knob, else `cpuinfo_max_freq`. The check had read
1140	  `cpuinfo_max_freq` with boost still on, 4673 on the 3900X, so `--pin-freq=4000` passed and the
1141	  kernel then capped the pin at 3801 once boost went off, a pin somewhere other than asked. A target
1142	  in that gap is refused naming the boost-off ceiling, and one past the hardware range as before
1143	- where a value is written decides how long it lasts, so no one-shot spelling exists: `no` in a file
1144	  is no opinion, the same as no key, so a lower file's pin still applies, while `--pin-freq=no`
1145	  skips every file's pin for one run. A host-wide pin in the XDG file is the unusual case this
1146	  gives up, a directory then needing the flag each run. `docs/config.md` splits the host's `[freq]`
1147	  and a run's `pin_freq` into two sections
1148	- a file's `pin_freq` is checked where its path is known, so a bad word names its file, and a `no`
1149	  is dropped there, so it neither overrides a lower file nor claims to be the source
1150	- `pin-freq`, the command, takes the same words, `pin-freq min_mhz`, and refuses `no`, pointing at
1151	  `restore-freq`
1152	- no flag writes a config file: a permanent change is an edit, since a run that edited its own
1153	  files would stop being reproducible from its command line, and the file a flag should edit is
1154	  ambiguous between the XDG and project-local layers
1155	- it resolves like every other run key, flag then file then default, so the `Config:` list and the
1156	  record name where the pin came from, `1745 MHz (config min_mhz) (iiac-perf.md)` for a directory's
1157	  pin and `no (--pin-freq, same as default)` for a run that skipped it
1158	- `suggest-freq` never takes a config's pin, since it pins each candidate itself, and says so on
1159	  the `pin_freq` line, while an explicit `--pin-freq` beside it is still refused
1160	- the pin source a run reports for an explicit frequency is `as given`, since the frequency may
1161	  now come from a file as well as the line
1162	- it resolves the "Two-regime runs" Todo entry (wink, 2026-08-17), which proposed this key as
1163	  `pin_freq = true|false` with a `--no-pin-freq` override. The words and `--pin-freq=no` replaced
1164	  both, so the entry retires here
1165	- a write refused for permission now prints its fix on a second line, naming the binary, `writing
1166	  cpufreq needs root, or the permissions \`iiac-perf-dev setup --apply\` grants` (wink, after a
1167	  sudo-less `--pin-freq` on the 3900X, which has no permissions installed yet)
1168	- tested without pinning: a scratch directory's `pin_freq` skipped by `--pin-freq=no`, a file's
1169	  `"no"`, bad values refused, and `max_mhz` and `4000` refused against the 3900X's real 3801 MHz
1170	  boost-off ceiling, all before any write. The sandbox's sysfs is read-only, so no pin ran here
1171	- first sudo-free run, the 3900X, 2026-09-15, by wink: `iiac-perf-dev setup --apply` created
1172	  `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` from the live state (1745-4673 MHz, boost on), installed the udev
1173	  rule, and took ownership of 122 files with one sudo, `/dev/cpu_dma_latency` the one more than the
1174	  sandbox counted. `iiac-perf-dev min-now --pin-freq` as the user then pinned at 3801, measured, and
1175	  restored with one settled line. On the 7600x the same day, with its own permissions and
1176	  `pin_mhz = 4701` declared, sudo-free `--pin-freq` pinned at 4701 (4.67 GHz delivered, at the
1177	  boost-off ceiling), `=3801` and `=4000` held theirs, `=no` ran unpinned at 5.44 GHz with boost on,
1178	  and each pin restored to `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`'s 2.99-5.46 GHz. Not yet shown: the rule
1179	  re-applying ownership after a reboot
1180	- after rebooting the 7600x (2026-09-15), wink's sudo-free `--pin-freq` pinned and restored with no
1181	  second `setup --apply`, so udev re-applied the ownership at boot
1182	- the restore report dropped `avg` and `base`: after a `--pin-freq=3300` run on the 7600x it read
1183	  `avg=2.99GHz`, an idle core at the bottom of its clamp, not the pin, which the warmup's
1184	  `3.29->3.29GHz` shows held. It reported 4.69, 3.80, or 2.99 by how fast the core idled. It now
1185	  prints what the restore set, governor, EPP, boost, and clamp, and `read-freq` and `pin-freq` keep

## Bugs

_See [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)._

## Closed

The last cycle's finished record, moved here whole by its closing commit and deleted by the next
opening ([Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). Earlier cycles are in the landmark commit's
copy of this section, and the cycles before the rule in the frozen [notes/chores/](notes/chores)
and [notes/done.md](notes/done.md).

### feat: config and setup

#### Problem

A run's parameters come from defaults, the XDG file, the project-local file, and flags, and the
report names neither every value nor where each came from, so two records cannot be checked for
matching parameters (wink, 2026-09-12). And a host is ready for iiac-perf only after hand work: its
`[freq]` declaration written with the clamp limits, and sudo for every `--pin-freq` and
`restore-freq` (wink, 2026-09-14). A missing limit is a live hazard, [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)'s
`restore-freq` entry: the 3900X has no XDG config, and its only declaration omits both limits.

#### Solution

A run says what configured it, a record carries it, a host is made ready by one command, and a
benchmark directory pins every run while every restore returns to the host's own steady state.

- **`Config:` list**: after `Setup:`, the files loaded and every run parameter with its value and

##### feat: a Config: list naming each value's source

The report names some parameters and none of their sources, so a reader cannot tell a default from
a file's value from a flag. A `Config:` list after `Setup:` names each.

- the loader records which file set each scalar key, the last overlay winning, so a source is known
  per key rather than per merged config
- one resolver, flag then file then default, returns every layered value with its source, and the
  `Config:` list is seventeen parameters: the eight config keys plus `samples`, `inner`, `pin_cpus`,
  `pin_freq`, `env_probe`, `ticks`, `inhibit`, `record`, and `tag`. `verbose` is left out, since it
  shapes logging and not the measurement
- names are the config keys' spelling, so the list, the file, and the coming record's `config`
  object share one vocabulary
- `same as default` compares rendered values, so `1-10 ms` in a file matches the built-in however
  the file spelled it
- `-D` shows the per-bench share with `--total-duration T over N benches` as its source, and a
  profile name shows its expansion, `smt = 0,12`
- `Setup:` keeps provenance about the box, the policy, the pins, and the inhibit state, and loses
  the block, warm-budget, and config-file lines to the list. The guide's quoted example outputs are
  historical and stay as they were

##### feat: the record carries the run's config

A record cannot be checked against another for matching parameters. Schema 6 adds a `config` object,
value and source per parameter, and the loaded files' paths.

- `config.params` is the `Config:` list keyed by name, each `{value, source, same_as_default}`,
  rendered as the report prints it, so the report and the record read alike. The numeric keys
  (`blocks`, `block_sleep_min_s`, ...) stay, so an analysis never parses `1-10 ms`
- `config.files` and a file source are absolute paths, since the project-local file loads relative
  to a directory the record does not otherwise name
- `pin_freq` records the resolved target and where it came from, `3801 MHz (base clock ...)`,
  where the list had printed `on` for a bare `--pin-freq`, so a record says what clock the run held
- the recorder is built after the list resolves, still before any bench runs, so a bad `--record`
  path fails as fast as before
- the host, the tags, and the config travel together as the recorder's per-process stamp, which
  keeps the record builder's argument list inside clippy's limit

##### fix: restore-freq refuses a declaration without clamp limits

A declaration without `min_mhz` and `max_mhz` restores to the hardware range. Refuse it and name
`setup`.

- the check sits in the steady-state resolver, so `restore-freq`, `pin-freq`, `--pin-freq`, and
  `suggest-freq` all refuse before any write, a pin needing its way home as much as a restore does
- the steady state's clamps are plain values now, so the restore plan has no hardware-range
  fallback left to reach
- the file still parses without the limits, the check living at use time like `epp` and `boost`,
  so a config that never pins is not broken by it
- `read-freq --as-config` printed the limits as an omitted comment, which the refusal would then
  reject, so it prints them from the live clamp in this rung, and comments them out when the clamp
  is pinned, since pasting a pin's `min = max` would make every restore a pin
- the refusal names `read-freq --as-config`, not `setup`, which does not exist until the next rung
  and joins the message there

##### feat: setup writes the host's freq declaration

A host's declaration is written by hand, and the hand forgets the limits. `setup` writes it from the
live state, clamp included.

- print by default and write with `--apply`, so the file is read before it exists
- never overwrite, where the opening planned an overwrite flag: a missing file is created, a file
  without `[freq]` gains the section at its end, and a file declaring `[freq]` is left alone and
  checked, since an XDG config may hold profiles and knobs a regenerated file would lose. The
  flag has nothing left to guard, so it does not exist
- the new text is parsed and passed through the same steady-state checks every pin and restore
  applies before anything is written, so a clamp pinned at setup time refuses instead of writing a
  pin as the steady state
- the `[freq]` lines come from the one builder `read-freq --as-config` prints, so the two cannot
  disagree, and both refusal messages now name `setup` first
- `setup` refuses to run as root, since under sudo `$HOME` may be root's and the file would land in
  the wrong home
- testing here: print-only against the real home, and `--apply` against a scratch
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` under the ignored `tmp/`, appending to a file with `blocks` and rechecking. The
  real `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` is wink's to write, the sandbox's `~/.config` being
  read-only

##### feat: setup installs and removes the udev permissions

Every pin and restore needs sudo. A udev rule granting the user ACLs on the cpufreq files and
`/dev/cpu_dma_latency` removes that, installed and removed by `setup`.

- ownership, not an ACL: the rule `chown`s each file to the user, since we think sysfs's POSIX ACL
  support is not reliable, while `chown` on sysfs files is ordinary udev practice. Unverified here,
  the sandbox's sysfs reading as `nobody`
- the rule is one `RUN` per knob on each CPU's `add` event, plus the global boost on `cpu0` and an
  `OWNER` on the latency device, so no shell quoting passes through udev and a knob a box lacks
  fails only its own line. It carries no `$`, which udev would expand
- the rule acts on boot and hotplug only, so `--apply` also takes ownership now, in one
  `sudo sh -c` script that writes the rule, reloads udev, and `chown`s. The script names each
  per-CPU knob once as a `cpu[0-9]*` glob, a 24-CPU box's 121 files reading as six lines
- print first everywhere: `setup` shows the root script, `--apply` runs it, `--uninstall` shows the
  removal, and `--uninstall --apply` removes the rule and gives the files back to root, leaving
  the config alone
- `USER` goes into the rule and the root script unquoted, so `setup` refuses a name that is not
  letters, digits, `_`, `.`, and `-`
- `setup` reports nothing to do when the rule file matches and the user owns every file, so a
  second `--apply` asks for no password
- the file list is the one the pin and restore plans write, exposed from `freqctl`, so the grant
  cannot drift from what the commands need. The `apply` hint and the help text now name setup's
  permissions beside root
- untested here: the sandbox cannot run sudo or write `/etc`, so the rule and scripts are checked
  as text, and wink's `--apply` on both hosts is the first real run

##### fix: setup checks a declared [freq] against the live state

Inserted after the trapezoid's push, at wink's direction, when the 7600x's `config.md` turned out to
hold the 3900X's clamp, 1745-4673 MHz against its live 2991-5457. `setup` passed it, since both
numbers fit the hardware range, so a restore there would cap the clock at 4.67 GHz. `setup` checks
a declaration against the live state, and the notes that recorded the wrong values are corrected.

- the comparison is the live state of the first CPU, the one `setup` declares from, and it covers
  every declared value: governor, EPP, boost, and both limits. A declared `min_mhz = max_mhz` is a
  legitimate steady state (wink, at this rung's review, pinning a benchmark host by config), so a
  live pin at the same value and boost matches it, and a live pin against a declared range names
  every difference with a note that a pin may still be running
- a mismatch fails `setup`, naming each value and printing the live section, and never rewrites
  the file: the fix is removing the table and rerunning `--apply`, or a `restore-freq` when the
  declaration is the intended state
- the steady-state check now holds `min_mhz` and `max_mhz` to a fixed-list driver's frequencies,
  as `pin_mhz` already was, so every clamp value a restore writes is one the driver lists. The
  other illegal values were refused already: zero and `min_mhz > max_mhz` at load, anything outside
  the hardware range at use
- the per-directory benchmark pin wink raised at the review, a project-local `[freq]` pin that
  would also decide where a restore returns, becomes a run key in a later rung of this cycle,
  `feat: pin_freq as a config key`, not a `[freq]` precedence trick
- run on the 7600x as a copy in `/tmp`: it named `min_mhz` 1745 against 2991 and `max_mhz` 4673
  against 5457. At wink's go the wrong file moved to `~/iiac-perf-data/` and `setup --apply` wrote
  the live state, after which `setup` reported the declaration matching. The permissions step
  failed at sudo, which needed a terminal, so no rule was installed and the files stayed root's
- the prose `setup` writes above the fence named `restore-freq` beside the table as if it were a
  key (wink, reading the new 7600x file). It now says the table is the steady state, that
  `iiac-perf restore-freq` sets the governor, EPP, boost, and clamp to it, and that every pin
  returns to it, and the 7600x's file was regenerated with that wording, its values unchanged
- notes corrected: the ops notes and the `restore-freq` bug entry had recorded 2991 and 5457 on
  2026-09-12, and the 3900X's record directories in `tmp/`, which the ops notes and three Todo
  entries cite, were found gone the same day, so those citations now say so

##### feat: say where the clock was restored to

Inserted at wink's direction, at the live-state rung's review. A restore prints nothing, and which
`[freq]` it used depends on the directory the run started in, so a user cannot tell where the clock
went back to. Every restore says so: the state read back and the file its `[freq]` came from, the
signal path printing the declared values it cannot read back. The `Config:` list and the record's
`config.params` gain a `freq` line, the declared table and its file or `(none declared)`, since a
`[freq]` set in a config showed nowhere in the report (wink, 2026-09-14, reading a run in the repo
directory whose `iiac-perf.md` declared one).

- one report after every restore's writes succeed: `freq: restored the [freq] from <file>:` and the
  state lines read back from sysfs, so the line says what the CPU holds rather than what was asked.
  `--pin-freq`'s guard, `suggest-freq`'s guard, and `restore-freq` share it, and `pin-freq` names
  the file its later `restore-freq` would use from the same directory
- the signal path prepares its line when the pin engages, the declared values and the file, and
  writes it with a bare `write` after the restore, marked as declared and not read back, since a
  handler may only write
- the loader records the file that set `[freq]` under `freq` beside the scalar keys' sources, which
  is what names the file in the report and in the `Config:` list
- `Config:` gains `freq`, the table as one line or `none declared`, and the record's
  `config.params` carries it the same way. A value past 24 characters no longer widens the value
  column, so the one long line leaves every other line's source where it was
- the read-back waits for the writes to land: wink's `sudo pin-freq` on the 3900X printed cpu0 at the
  plan's 563 MHz staging floor and cpu1-23 at the old 1745 floor, while `read-freq` seconds later
  showed 3801-3801 everywhere. The kernel applies amd-pstate limit changes after the write returns,
  so every report now polls each written file every 10 ms, up to a second, until it reads back the
  last token written, frequencies matching within 1 MHz, and says `not settled` naming the file
  when one has not. `pin-freq`'s own lines wait the same way, and a pinned run and `suggest-freq`
  wait silently before measuring, warning only when the pin has not landed
- a pin in place broke the next pin: `--pin-freq` refused `max_mhz 4673` as outside `563-3801`,
  because `cpuinfo_max_freq` reads the nominal frequency while boost is off. The declared limits are
  now checked against the boosted ceiling, `amd_pstate_max_freq` where the driver exposes it, else
  `cpuinfo_max_freq`, and a pin's target keeps the ceiling as it reads, since a pin turns boost off.
  Without this, `restore-freq` itself would have refused to leave a pin once limits were declared
- tested live on the 3900X by wink with the rung's first build: `sudo pin-freq` printed the
  unsettled lines that led to the wait, and `--pin-freq` hit the ceiling bug. The settle and ceiling
  logic are tested with a fake reader and a pinned-ceiling fixture. With the fixed build, wink's
  `sudo iiac-perf-dev min-now -d 1 --pin-freq`, started while the box was still pinned, passed the
  declared 4673 against the boosted ceiling, pinned at 3801, and ended with `freq: restored the
  [freq] from iiac-perf.md:` over one settled state line, boost on and 1.75-4.67 GHz, which
  `read-freq` then matched (2026-09-15). The Ctrl-C line is tested by its text only

##### feat: pin_freq as a config key

Inserted at wink's direction, at the same review. A benchmark directory can pin the clock only by
declaring `min_mhz = max_mhz` in a project-local `[freq]`, which also moves where every restore
returns. A `pin_freq` run key, the config twin of `--pin-freq`, pins every run and restores to the
host's steady state on exit, a number for MHz or a word naming the host's value, and
`--pin-freq=no` skips a config's pin for one run.

- the values (wink, at this rung's review): a number for MHz, or a word naming the host's `[freq]`
  value to pin at, `pin_mhz` (else the base clock, and the bare flag) or `min_mhz`, and `no` for no
  pin. The same text works in the file and on the line, a quoted `"3801"` included. Booleans and
  `on`/`off` were tried and dropped: `pin_freq` is which frequency, not a switch, and a word naming
  the key says which. `max_mhz` is a word too (wink: if `min_mhz` is, `max_mhz` should be), pinning
  whenever the declared value fits under the boost-off ceiling
- every pin target is checked against the ceiling with boost off, which a pin turns off: the base
  clock where the box has a boost knob, else `cpuinfo_max_freq`. The check had read
  `cpuinfo_max_freq` with boost still on, 4673 on the 3900X, so `--pin-freq=4000` passed and the
  kernel then capped the pin at 3801 once boost went off, a pin somewhere other than asked. A target
  in that gap is refused naming the boost-off ceiling, and one past the hardware range as before
- where a value is written decides how long it lasts, so no one-shot spelling exists: `no` in a file
  is no opinion, the same as no key, so a lower file's pin still applies, while `--pin-freq=no`
  skips every file's pin for one run. A host-wide pin in the XDG file is the unusual case this
  gives up, a directory then needing the flag each run. `docs/config.md` splits the host's `[freq]`
  and a run's `pin_freq` into two sections
- a file's `pin_freq` is checked where its path is known, so a bad word names its file, and a `no`
  is dropped there, so it neither overrides a lower file nor claims to be the source
- `pin-freq`, the command, takes the same words, `pin-freq min_mhz`, and refuses `no`, pointing at
  `restore-freq`
- no flag writes a config file: a permanent change is an edit, since a run that edited its own
  files would stop being reproducible from its command line, and the file a flag should edit is
  ambiguous between the XDG and project-local layers
- it resolves like every other run key, flag then file then default, so the `Config:` list and the
  record name where the pin came from, `1745 MHz (config min_mhz) (iiac-perf.md)` for a directory's
  pin and `no (--pin-freq, same as default)` for a run that skipped it
- `suggest-freq` never takes a config's pin, since it pins each candidate itself, and says so on
  the `pin_freq` line, while an explicit `--pin-freq` beside it is still refused
- the pin source a run reports for an explicit frequency is `as given`, since the frequency may
  now come from a file as well as the line
- it resolves the "Two-regime runs" Todo entry (wink, 2026-08-17), which proposed this key as
  `pin_freq = true|false` with a `--no-pin-freq` override. The words and `--pin-freq=no` replaced
  both, so the entry retires here
- a write refused for permission now prints its fix on a second line, naming the binary, `writing
  cpufreq needs root, or the permissions \`iiac-perf-dev setup --apply\` grants` (wink, after a
  sudo-less `--pin-freq` on the 3900X, which has no permissions installed yet)
- tested without pinning: a scratch directory's `pin_freq` skipped by `--pin-freq=no`, a file's
  `"no"`, bad values refused, and `max_mhz` and `4000` refused against the 3900X's real 3801 MHz
  boost-off ceiling, all before any write. The sandbox's sysfs is read-only, so no pin ran here
- first sudo-free run, the 3900X, 2026-09-15, by wink: `iiac-perf-dev setup --apply` created
  `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md` from the live state (1745-4673 MHz, boost on), installed the udev
  rule, and took ownership of 122 files with one sudo, `/dev/cpu_dma_latency` the one more than the
  sandbox counted. `iiac-perf-dev min-now --pin-freq` as the user then pinned at 3801, measured, and
  restored with one settled line. On the 7600x the same day, with its own permissions and
  `pin_mhz = 4701` declared, sudo-free `--pin-freq` pinned at 4701 (4.67 GHz delivered, at the
  boost-off ceiling), `=3801` and `=4000` held theirs, `=no` ran unpinned at 5.44 GHz with boost on,
  and each pin restored to `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.md`'s 2.99-5.46 GHz. Not yet shown: the rule
  re-applying ownership after a reboot
- after rebooting the 7600x (2026-09-15), wink's sudo-free `--pin-freq` pinned and restored with no
  second `setup --apply`, so udev re-applied the ownership at boot
- the restore report dropped `avg` and `base`: after a `--pin-freq=3300` run on the 7600x it read
  `avg=2.99GHz`, an idle core at the bottom of its clamp, not the pin, which the warmup's
  `3.29->3.29GHz` shows held. It reported 4.69, 3.80, or 2.99 by how fast the core idled. It now

  the live average. The run's clock belongs in the report's stats instead, filed as the Todo entry

236	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / commit)

238	([why](rationale.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit))
239	
240	A ladder step and its commit description share a *title* shape, a [Conventional
241	Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`, an optional
242	`(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in
243	the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the [Commit-body
244	form](#commit-body-form), the ladder's are conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
245	above). The shared template:
246	
247	```
248	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`

251	    <optional prose intro>
252	      - <optional sub-item>
253	      ...
254	```

256	The two surfaces apply it as:
257	
258	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title

260	  closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker. Its position in the
261	  list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its text says so. Detail
262	  lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection headed by the rung's exact
263	  title (see the protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
264	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose (see
265	  [Commit description](../AGENTS.md#commit-description)).
266	
267	The title is **identical** across both for a given step, so a step's ladder entry and its commit
268	title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection heading carries the same title, a third
269	surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
270	protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
271	
272	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct descriptive
273	title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The block's title heading carries
274	the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the bookends below). To keep a
275	cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem
276	(e.g. `config loader`).
277	
278	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a suffix, "
279	opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
280	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
281	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the block's title heading carries
282	it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the closing rung's subsection anchor
283	clear of the title heading's. A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare
284	title, in both repos and in its one ladder rung ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The type
285	repeats across the pair even though the bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make
286	them scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.

288	### Commit titles and descriptions
289	
290	([why](rationale.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions))
291	
292	The vocabulary over the structure: [Conventional-commit
293	shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) holds what a title and body are shaped like, and
294	this section holds what may fill them. The title is a [Conventional
295	Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), `<type>: <short description>` with an optional
296	`(scope)`, at the width in [Line widths](#line-widths). The body is the [Commit-body
297	form](#commit-body-form), wrapped per Line widths, with no version in title or body, no file list,
298	and no deliberation. `vc-x1 push` gives both repos' commits the same title and body. `ochid:` is
299	the body's last line, stamped by push, and a breaking change uses the hyphenated
300	`BREAKING-CHANGE:` trailer key.
301	
302	#### Conventional commit types
303	
304	The common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`. A type beyond the common set
305	is a declared one ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)), and a title check admits
306	exactly the two vocabularies.
307	
308	#### Conventional commit scopes
309	
310	A scope names a component as its user would name it (a subcommand, a repo), never a file or
311	directory, and is omitted when there is none. A declared type's scope slot carries its
312	declaration's vocabulary instead ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)).
313	
314	#### Project-declared types
315	
316	Beyond the common types, a project may declare its own when a recurring kind of work deserves one
317	searchable token. The declaration names the type, its scope vocabulary, and its description
318	grammar, so a reader can parse the titles and a title check can admit them by name, and the scope
319	slot then carries what the declaration says rather than a component. A project's own declarations
320	live in its `custom.md`, and the set declares for itself:
321	
322	- `agent-files`, the set's own lifecycle: `agent-files(<scope>): vX.Y.Z`, the description being the
323	  agent-files version in its `v` spelling ([Agent-files
324	  version](versioning.md#agent-files-version)), which keeps the formulaic titles unique and is the
325	  one version a title may carry ([Versions live in the version-of-record
326	  only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)).
327	  - The two scopes:
328	    - `proposal`, outbound work for others to adopt. The cycle bumps the agent-files version, and
329	      the title names the new one.
330	    - `adoption`, inbound. The cycle copies the source's version file, and the title names what it
331	      took.
332	  - Who proposed to whom, or adopted from whom, is the message record's `from:` and `to:`, never
333	    the title's.
334	  - `git log --grep 'agent-files('` finds every agent-files title, the recurring type being the
335	    token that collects the thread.

337	### Steps are named, not numbered
338	
339	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a
340	rung's place in the list already *is* its place in the ladder, so a number beside it would restate
341	the position and then have to be maintained.
342	
343	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
344	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
345	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable where a title is
346	  resolved: within its own cycle's block, so a ladder rung names one step and its subsection heading
347	  one anchor, since a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first one. Across the repo's history a
348	  title may repeat.
349	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and nothing
350	  else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder come along.

363	types](#project-declared-types)): it names an agreed text, not a build, and naming which is the
364	title's job.
365

The two surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title
  reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the
  closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker. Its position in the
  list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its text says so. Detail
  lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection headed by the rung's exact
  title (see the protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose (see
  [Commit description](../AGENTS.md#commit-description)).

The title is **identical** across both for a given step, so a step's ladder entry and its commit
title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection heading carries the same title, a third
surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct descriptive
title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The block's title heading carries
the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the bookends below). To keep a
cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem
(e.g. `config loader`).

**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a suffix, "
opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the block's title heading carries
it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the closing rung's subsection anchor
clear of the title heading's. A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare
title, in both repos and in its one ladder rung ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The type
repeats across the pair even though the bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make
them scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.

### Commit titles and descriptions

([why](rationale.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions))

The vocabulary over the structure: [Conventional-commit
shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) holds what a title and body are shaped like, and
this section holds what may fill them. The title is a [Conventional
Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), `<type>: <short description>` with an optional
`(scope)`, at the width in [Line widths](#line-widths). The body is the [Commit-body
form](#commit-body-form), wrapped per Line widths, with no version in title or body, no file list,
and no deliberation. `vc-x1 push` gives both repos' commits the same title and body. `ochid:` is
the body's last line, stamped by push, and a breaking change uses the hyphenated
`BREAKING-CHANGE:` trailer key.

#### Conventional commit types

The common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`. A type beyond the common set
is a declared one ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)), and a title check admits
exactly the two vocabularies.

#### Conventional commit scopes

A scope names a component as its user would name it (a subcommand, a repo), never a file or
directory, and is omitted when there is none. A declared type's scope slot carries its
declaration's vocabulary instead ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)).

#### Project-declared types

Beyond the common types, a project may declare its own when a recurring kind of work deserves one
searchable token. The declaration names the type, its scope vocabulary, and its description
grammar, so a reader can parse the titles and a title check can admit them by name, and the scope
slot then carries what the declaration says rather than a component. A project's own declarations
live in its `custom.md`, and the set declares for itself:

- `agent-files`, the set's own lifecycle: `agent-files(<scope>): vX.Y.Z`, the description being the
  agent-files version in its `v` spelling ([Agent-files
  version](versioning.md#agent-files-version)), which keeps the formulaic titles unique and is the
  one version a title may carry ([Versions live in the version-of-record
  only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)).
  - The two scopes:
    - `proposal`, outbound work for others to adopt. The cycle bumps the agent-files version, and
      the title names the new one.
    - `adoption`, inbound. The cycle copies the source's version file, and the title names what it
      took.
  - Who proposed to whom, or adopted from whom, is the message record's `from:` and `to:`, never
    the title's.
  - `git log --grep 'agent-files('` finds every agent-files title, the recurring type being the
    token that collects the thread.

### Steps are named, not numbered

A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a
rung's place in the list already *is* its place in the ladder, so a number beside it would restate
the position and then have to be maintained.

- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable where a title is
  resolved: within its own cycle's block, so a ladder rung names one step and its subsection heading
  one anchor, since a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first one. Across the repo's history a
  title may repeat.
- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and nothing
  else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder come along.
  See [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark).
- **`## Todo` is ordered, not numbered**: priority is file order ([Todo
  format](notes.md#todo-format)), so no rank number exists to be cited (the numbered form retired
  2026-08-27).

### Versions live in the version-of-record only

No version appears in durable prose: not in a ladder rung, a commit title, or a commit body. The
manifest is the version's only written home (see [versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's
version is read from that file at that commit
([why](rationale.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)). The one exception is the set's
own version in an `agent-files` title, wherever that title appears ([Project-declared
types](#project-declared-types)): it names an agreed text, not a build, and naming which is the
title's job.

**No surface records a version.** Which commit a version names is read from the manifest at that
commit, and "what shipped in 0.42.0" is answered by `git log` on the manifest, not by a list kept in
prose. The earlier chores as-built rungs and `## Done` entries carried versions beside commit SHAs,
and retired with the records they lived in ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## Agent-files name no project

An agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names an adopter, an adopter's history, or an
adopter's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every adopter shares and stay.
What is barred is an adopter's repo appearing in universal text
([why](rationale.md#agent-files-name-no-project)).

**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the agent-file, and leave the evidence trail
in the records of the project that earned it (the cycle-record, Todo entries), reachable from the
commit that changed the agent-file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not an adopter. A
specimen in the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
reference, per the same distinction [Versions live in the version-of-record
only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only) draws.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the agent writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, the cycle-record) should stick
to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal
claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a reader can tell the
measured from the inferred ([why](rationale.md#speculation-marker)).

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with "We think ..."
(or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins because Y caches
better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a prediction ("this should scale
linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.

  `--unshare-pid`, so a background spinner started in one
  shell is invisible to every other one — `pgrep`/`pkill`
  silently find nothing and cannot stop it. The only reliable
  "machine is quiet again" signal is the `timeout` expiring.

  before this was understood (2026-07-25). Related: an
  unpinned bench run on the machine hosting the bot session

  fitting the hardware range. `setup --apply` rewrote it from the
  live state on 2026-09-14 to `2991` and `5457`, the wrong file
  kept as `~/iiac-perf-data/config.md-3900x-clamp-20260914`.

#### Problem

bench's level, so a run's CI95 and LSC, computed over blocks inside one process, are lower bounds
that can miss the real spread by a wide margin (wink, 2026-09-05, confirmed 2026-09-12).

- **the evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-12 (UTC 2026-09-13), `zcr-mpsc-v1-2t -d 5`, 100 blocks,
  1-10 ms sleep, config isolated. Records in the 7600x's `~/iiac-perf-data/warmup-20260913/`, a copy
  and its `analyze.py` once in this repo's ignored `tmp/warmup-7600x-20260913/`, lost
  2026-09-14 (the ops notes' kept-records bullet):
  - one process running the bench four times, three processes: every process read run 1 at 60.4 to
    60.6 ns, run 2 at 62.6 to 63.0, run 3 at 71.7 to 71.9, and run 4 at 63.4 or 71.7, each run
    claiming CI95 under 0.1 ns. The plain 0.28.10 showed its own run-indexed levels, 59.8 to 68.1 ns
  - pinned 0,1, fresh processes read 60.6 to 60.7 ns three times and 76.0 once, and unpinned 63.4
    to 63.6 ns four times
  - the plain 0.28.10 against the dev 0.28.11, pinned: 67.9 against 60.8 ns on the zcr bench and
    16.36 against 16.35 ns on `min-now`, so the harness measures alike and the gap is the binary's
    placement level
  - block warmup 0, 2, and 10 ms, pinned 0,1, three interleaved each: means 60.58, 60.45, and 60.62
    ns, no effect, 10 ms costing 0.9 s a run
- **the earlier evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-05, `zcr-spsc-v1-2t --inner 100 --blocks 10
  --pin-cpus 2,8`: five invocations with 1 s block sleeps and 100 ms warmups each held their ten
  blocks within 0.1 ns, and the invocations landed on two levels 0.15 ns apart, seven times the
  spread the blocks predicted. CPUs N and N+6 are SMT siblings on the 7600x, so `2,8` was a
  one-core run

#### Solution

iiac-perf finds a bench's CI95 and LSC itself: every bench of the list runs in its own child
process, `runs` times, back to back, and the error bars are computed over the process means beside
the within-process ones.

- **the bench list as a setting**: the positional `BENCHES`, `--benches`, and a `benches` config
  key, so a config file can name what runs
- **one bench per process**: the parent respawns `current_exe()` once per run, as
  `qualify-environment` does, is inert while a child runs, and starts the sleep inhibit and the
  clock pin once for all of them. A child gets `--pin-cpus` and every run knob, runs one bench, and
  hands its results back as a record
- **replication**: `--runs N` and a `runs` config key, default 5, and `--run-sleep` with a
  `run_sleep` key, a time or a random range between runs, replacing `qualify-environment`'s `--gap`
- **one statistics owner**: CI95 and LSC over a series of means is one module, fed block means
  within a process and process means across them, which the "Analyze a directory of records" entry
  reuses
- **the output**: a line per run as each child finishes, then the bench's summary with both tiers.
  `-v` shows each child's full report
- **the labels**: "block" names the within-process replicate and "run" the between-process one, so
  the rows read `CI95 blocks`, `LSC blocks`, `CI95 runs`, and `LSC runs`, and a record carries a
  series id grouping one invocation's children

#### Acceptance check

On the 3900X, `iiac-perf-dev zcr-mpsc-v0-2t zcr-mpsc-v1-2t --runs 3 --pin-cpus 0,1 -d 2 --record
<dir>` writes six records with six distinct pids and one series id, each bench's three runs back to
back, and prints for each bench a line per run and its mean, `CI95 blocks`, `LSC blocks`, `CI95
runs`, and `LSC runs`. The same list given as a `benches` key in a config file runs the same
benches. A unit test reproduces the design notes' worked LSC, about 131 ns at n=3 from the six-run
series. `vc-x1 validate` passes.

### One bench per process, CI95 and LSC across processes

A process start re-rolls where the rings and stacks land in memory, and that placement sets a
bench's level, so a run's CI95 and LSC, computed over blocks inside one process, are lower bounds
that can miss the real spread by a wide margin (wink, 2026-09-05, confirmed 2026-09-12). iiac-perf
should find a bench's CI95 and LSC itself: one bench per process by default, replicated across
fresh processes, interleaved A/B, the error bars computed over process means.

- **the evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-12 (UTC 2026-09-13), `zcr-mpsc-v1-2t -d 5`, 100 blocks,
  1-10 ms sleep, config isolated. Records in the 7600x's `~/iiac-perf-data/warmup-20260913/`, a copy
  and its `analyze.py` once in this repo's ignored `tmp/warmup-7600x-20260913/`, lost
  2026-09-14 (the ops notes' kept-records bullet):
  - one process running the bench four times, three processes: every process read run 1 at 60.4 to
    60.6 ns, run 2 at 62.6 to 63.0, run 3 at 71.7 to 71.9, and run 4 at 63.4 or 71.7, each run
    claiming CI95 under 0.1 ns. The plain 0.28.10 showed its own run-indexed levels, 59.8 to 68.1 ns
  - pinned 0,1, fresh processes read 60.6 to 60.7 ns three times and 76.0 once, and unpinned 63.4
    to 63.6 ns four times
  - the plain 0.28.10 against the dev 0.28.11, pinned: 67.9 against 60.8 ns on the zcr bench and
    16.36 against 16.35 ns on `min-now`, so the harness measures alike and the gap is the binary's
    placement level
  - block warmup 0, 2, and 10 ms, pinned 0,1, three interleaved each: means 60.58, 60.45, and 60.62
    ns, no effect, 10 ms costing 0.9 s a run
- **the earlier evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-05, `zcr-spsc-v1-2t --inner 100 --blocks 10
  --pin-cpus 2,8`: five invocations with 1 s block sleeps and 100 ms warmups each held their ten
  blocks within 0.1 ns, and the invocations landed on two levels 0.15 ns apart, seven times the
  spread the blocks predicted. CPUs N and N+6 are SMT siblings on the 7600x, so `2,8` was a
  one-core run
- **one bench per process**: a bench list, `all` included, runs each bench in its own child, so no
  bench inherits another's placement and the run-indexed levels above cannot appear. The parent
  respawns `current_exe()` as `qualify-environment` does, is inert while a child runs, the
  `suggest-freq` sampler bug in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md) being the warning, and passes its config
  so knobs and pins match
- **replication across processes**: N children per bench, A and B alternating when comparing, the
  guide's standing advice done by the tool. The CI95 and LSC over process means are the first that
  are not lower bounds, and a child needs a second or two since blocks within a process agree to
  0.1%
- **one statistics owner**: CI95 and LSC over a series of means is one module, fed block means
  within a process and process means across them, and the same arithmetic serves `analyze` over a
  directory of records (the "Analyze a directory of records" entry's cross-run tier)
- **error-bar labels**: a single-process CI95 and LSC print labeled within-process, and an
  across-process row joins them once spawning exists, the ratio of the two saying whether
  per-process state dominates. "Block" keeps the within-process replicate, and the between-process
  one gets its own word, so a row never has to say which it meant
- **naming the level** is a second experiment: children that map the ring regions themselves and
  sweep the second ring's page offset against the first, then huge pages. We think it is cache-set
  aliasing from placement

  records' host block makes the start of the cross-host comparison, and a run of the mpsc v1 pair

### Qualification reports evidence, not verdicts

Retire the prejudging NOT QUALIFIED stamp (wink, 2026-08-02) in favor of measured statements a
reader judges.

- blocks-based: A/A repeatability (does a same-code delta clear LSC?), CI95/LSC as the
  published sensitivity ("this box resolves X ns on this bench"), stratification by state
  instead of a blended letter
- the 3900X reads NOT QUALIFIED today for mid-run bistable transitions warmup cannot
  prevent: a trait to report, not a disqualification. The 7600x dwell case that motivated
  the gate is fixed by the dynamic-warmup cycle
- entangled with "Qualify the environment without a bench" (below) and machine-readable
  output, and it wants the blocks-knobs entry (above) landed first

### Seam-clock attribution

Sample `cpuinfo_avg_freq` at block seams (the reader exists, `src/freq.rs`) so a mid-run step
gets a "clock moved" label, the way warmup now separates a dwell from the top. Also the natural
home for surfacing the clock ratio in normal output as one coherent story (chores-06: the 3900X
flip at ~2-4 s is almost certainly a visible clock move).

- the sampling half moved into the measure-reproducibility cycle's record rung (2026-08-16):
  seam samples join the record, per-block/per-run frequency stats fall out, and the pin
  verifies itself. What stays here is the report surface, the "clock moved" label
- the ~2-4 s flip is no longer a guess: 0.26.0-1's settle state named the states directly,
  4.09 GHz entry and ~4.53 GHz top on the 3900x under today's policy

### Qualify the environment without a bench

`qualify-environment` respawns children running `min-now`, but every number in its table comes
from the micro-probe series, which never touches the bench. The bench is there only to give the
warm something to do and to produce a report to parse, so the selftest inherits a workload's
character it does not want, and the parent parses prose (see the machine-readable-output entry
below, which this would make moot for the selftest).

- measure the probe series directly: warm and probe with no bench registered, grade the
  stretches, done. The `mean` column becomes the probe's own floor, which is the quantity the
  grade is computed from rather than a second measurement of nearly the same thing
- **the warm's character is the open question.** A probe-driven warm is light. On hardware
  where a heavy workload drives a different clock/power state (AVX offsets), a light warm
  would qualify the box for work it will not do. Moot on the 3900X and 7600x, where `min-now`
  *is* essentially the probe, so decide it with a measurement on a box where it isn't
- **respawn or loop** is a second question, not this one: respawning resets process-local
  state (address space, caches, allocator) and loops do not, but neither resets the machine's
  P-state. What re-rolls that is the gap and the duty cycle. If the answer is loop, the
  results stay structured data and never become text
- coordinate with the "Dynamic warmup" Todo, which owns the convergence rule this would warm
  by, and with the grade-block columns entry, which reformats the table this prints [[75]]

25	A process start re-rolls where the rings and stacks land in memory, and that placement sets a
26	bench's level, so a run's CI95 and LSC, computed over blocks inside one process, are lower bounds
27	that can miss the real spread by a wide margin (wink, 2026-09-05, confirmed 2026-09-12).
28	
29	- **the evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-12 (UTC 2026-09-13), `zcr-mpsc-v1-2t -d 5`, 100 blocks,
30	  1-10 ms sleep, config isolated. Records in the 7600x's `~/iiac-perf-data/warmup-20260913/`, a copy
31	  and its `analyze.py` once in this repo's ignored `tmp/warmup-7600x-20260913/`, lost
32	  2026-09-14 (the ops notes' kept-records bullet):
33	  - one process running the bench four times, three processes: every process read run 1 at 60.4 to
34	    60.6 ns, run 2 at 62.6 to 63.0, run 3 at 71.7 to 71.9, and run 4 at 63.4 or 71.7, each run
35	    claiming CI95 under 0.1 ns. The plain 0.28.10 showed its own run-indexed levels, 59.8 to 68.1 ns
36	  - pinned 0,1, fresh processes read 60.6 to 60.7 ns three times and 76.0 once, and unpinned 63.4
37	    to 63.6 ns four times
38	  - the plain 0.28.10 against the dev 0.28.11, pinned: 67.9 against 60.8 ns on the zcr bench and
39	    16.36 against 16.35 ns on `min-now`, so the harness measures alike and the gap is the binary's
40	    placement level
41	  - block warmup 0, 2, and 10 ms, pinned 0,1, three interleaved each: means 60.58, 60.45, and 60.62
42	    ns, no effect, 10 ms costing 0.9 s a run
43	- **the earlier evidence**, the 7600x on 2026-09-05, `zcr-spsc-v1-2t --inner 100 --blocks 10
44	  --pin-cpus 2,8`: five invocations with 1 s block sleeps and 100 ms warmups each held their ten
45	  blocks within 0.1 ns, and the invocations landed on two levels 0.15 ns apart, seven times the
46	  spread the blocks predicted. CPUs N and N+6 are SMT siblings on the 7600x, so `2,8` was a
47	  one-core run
48	
49	#### Solution
50	
51	iiac-perf finds a bench's CI95 and LSC itself: every bench of the list runs in its own child
52	process, `runs` times, back to back, and the error bars are computed over the process means beside
53	the within-process ones.
54	
55	- **the bench list as a setting**: the positional `BENCHES`, `--benches`, and a `benches` config
56	  key, so a config file can name what runs
57	- **one bench per process**: the parent respawns `current_exe()` once per run, as
58	  `qualify-environment` does, and starts the sleep inhibit and the clock pin once for all of them.
59	  It is inert while a child runs, the `suggest-freq` sampler bug in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md) being
60	  the warning. A child gets `--pin-cpus` and every run knob, runs one bench, and hands its results
61	  back as a record
62	- **replication**: `--runs N` and a `runs` config key, default 5, and `--run-sleep` with a
63	  `run_sleep` key, a time or a random range between runs, replacing `qualify-environment`'s `--gap`.
64	  A child needs a second or two, since blocks within a process agree to 0.1%
65	- **one statistics owner**: CI95 and LSC over a series of means is one module, fed block means
66	  within a process and process means across them, which the "Analyze a directory of records" entry
67	  reuses
68	- **the output**: a line per run as each child finishes, then the bench's summary with both tiers.
69	  `-v` shows each child's full report
70	- **the labels**: "block" names the within-process replicate and "run" the between-process one, so
71	  the rows read `CI95 blocks`, `LSC blocks`, `CI95 runs`, and `LSC runs`, their ratio saying
72	  whether per-process state dominates, and a record carries a series id grouping one invocation's
73	  children
